text:
Erin Burnett: CNN is learning the National Security Agency's network outage, still not resolved for a second day, is now affecting a critical intelligence facility. Four sources tonight telling CNN that the outage is affecting a Georgia facility which supports signals intelligence and cybersecurity operations focused on the Middle East, alarming on every level, including that the United States is engaged in war with Iran. Attacks on tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz have surged in recent weeks and today, just today, Iran targeted a Kuwaiti air base that hosts U.S. forces, U.S. soldiers on the ground. And U.S. intelligence sources also tell CNN that Iran is developing a plot to target senior Trump officials. We've reported on that earlier this week, perhaps with a dirty bomb in Washington. Adding to the fear, U.S. officials in a worldwide threats hearing today on Capitol Hill, which was held as the United States has faced six major network outages in six days, say that Iran is posing a real threat at this time. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin in his written testimony writes, quote, Iranian activity has increasingly targeted the transportation, health care, water, energy and financial services sectors, I'm sorry, which basically is a list of all of the areas that have seen outages in the past few days and all the major sectors that Americans need to survive. And when it comes to these outages, the Trump administration continues, they say, to be in the dark on what caused them. The root cause of what happened, we don't have clarity yet. If we were subject to a hack, we will share that with you. Meantime, the Homeland Security Secretary, Markwayne Mullin, stands by his decision to fly with his family to the LSU Texas football game in a government plane as thousands and thousands and thousands of other Americans were stuck sleeping on airport floors dealing with the nationwide ground stop fallout on Saturday.

Markwayne Mullin: I wanted to be a good uncle and take my little niece who's never been to LSU games. We had discussions at 10 o'clock Saturday morning. Should we cancel it? We had deep conversations about it and it came in that if we cancel something with the airspace was completely open, it could bring confusion because I was meeting the governor there, I was meeting other people there that would show maybe distrust that we're not even willing to fly.

Erin Burnett: Or maybe it would have shown good judgment. And even Republicans are taking Mullin to task. Here's Congressman Massie to TMZ DC today. Listen to him. Listen to his press conferences.

Thomas Massie: He's not instilling confidence. You think he doesn't have a handle on this situation or any, you don't have faith in him to... I don't think he could understand the answer if somebody gave it to him.

Erin Burnett: So how's he going to tell us what's actually going on? Well, Republican Senator John Kennedy is another one who didn't hold back when it comes to the Trump administration's handling of the outages.

John Kennedy: The jackassery and the seat up here is especially deep. It's so deep sometimes I think I'm going to drown in it. Drowning in jackassery.

Erin Burnett: Well, he never mince his words. And here's another important thing. As the U.S. faces outages which have caused public disruption and fear, the director of the FBI, Kash Patel, did not even attend today's worldwide threats hearing. He's the director of the FBI, an FBI which, by the way, is involved in investigating the outages. They've even picked up the wires and all those things from the FAA and FBI hands. Well, the Republican chairman says that he invited Patel to testify at the hearing months ago. But the FBI chief decided to no show. And as for no shows, Vice President J.D. Vance pulled out of a marquee New York Times event, the Deal Book Summit, at the last minute today using the outages as an excuse for a close to unprecedented last minute cancellation. His office tells us, quote, the vice president has been asked to attend meetings amid the wave of outages that have affected a series of industries in recent days. Well, the V.P.'s backing out and public silence today was, of course, a stark contrast to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who was eager to jump into the void last night, making this statement from the Philippines. People are nervous and they're anxious.

Marco Rubio: I wanted to come here today this morning to offer just full transparency.

Erin Burnett: Of course, those words come again as the administration says it does not know what did cause the outages, even as they say that they know maybe what didn't. And Trump himself downplays it all, saying, quote, it's fine. I want to go now to the Democratic Senator Ruben Gallego, who sits on the Homeland Security Committee. And I appreciate your time, Senator. So how worried are you and what are you being briefed on or aware of about this outage at the NSA that continues? And now with this new detail of it affecting the system used for Mideast intelligence.

Ruben Gallego: Well, not enough information is being shared, especially for people who have oversight. And I think we should be concerned. This is a very high level of encryption. Some of our best levels of communication happen through these channels. So we should be fairly scared that someone has capability to do this. This is kind of a bigger problem that we're having right now. If you're seeing with a kind of the horrible kind of tech infrastructure in this country right now, it's starting to break down. Some of it supposedly is mechanical. Some of it can be from malcontents and can be from other types of potentially bad agents. And so what it really costs is for this this administration to be on the ball, start actually updating and upgrading our systems, getting together and getting a good policy to really get us ready for a future fight. Because right now it does not look like we are ready for it. No, it doesn't. And the American public at least feels that sense of insecurity and lack of preparedness. And the NSA outage is far from the only one. Maybe that's why people feel this way. Microsoft, banks, Chase payment systems, Apple, hospitals, the hospital, right. Everything. Right. And I want to play what some of what just some of what the Trump administration senator has been saying over just the past day about what's causing all of this. Based on what we know today, after a great deal of diligence, these are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes. They are not a coordinated or state sponsored attack. We have zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyber hackers, with criminals, with another nation state, with a malign actor of any kind. Obviously, they're saying that, but they're also saying they don't know what is causing it, right. So it does, the gap between those two things is not necessarily confidence inspiring. Are you confident that they know what they're saying when they are adamant that it's not a state actor? I unfortunately am not confident. And what should scare other people is the fact that there's a lot of people that have even less information than me that are just relying right now on the government to be functioning. I get text messages from my big family all the time every time they hear anything like what does this mean? I was stuck on food. I got to get some water to get money out. The fact that these are the conversations Americans are having all the time tells you that there's a lack of confidence and the president and his administration need to be actively trying to encourage confidence. And again, this is not a partisan thing. This is not me trying to be a bad Democrat or a good Democrat to attack Republicans. I want the American public to have confidence right now. And these guys are not creating an air of confidence whatsoever.

Erin Burnett: How concerned are you about the sort of the volume of the outages we're seeing? And you know, we're mentioning some of the big names, but there's a lot of smaller names that are being targeted as well. But the big names are in every single of the most important crucial life, you know, reliant sectors of the country.

Cynthia Kaiser: I am incredibly concerned at the volume we've seen because there's probably a mixture here of technical outages, the everyday hacks targeting that are happening to organizations across the U.S., across the world. And it really shows that it may not even matter, right? Whether it's a hacker, whether it's an outage, it's disrupting all of us. It's disrupting operations. It's like how we actually engage in the digital economy and everything we depend on. It shows how interconnected everything's become that a small problem can have these outside consequences. It's exposing a weakness and an inability to recover.

Erin Burnett: David, you know, a moment ago when we played Marco Rubio and Jay Clayton, they were saying these are all separate and they have nothing to do with nefarious actors, even as the administration says they do not know what is causing this. They say it's not those things because the tactics being used in these instances are not what they've seen nefarious actors use before. Does that add up to you?

David Kennedy: Yeah. Yeah, Erin, I don't think anybody knows what's going on right now. And I guess I don't, you know, going back to Cynthia's point, I don't know what's worse. If our infrastructure can't stay stable during normal patch outages or patch updates, that's a major problem. I'd probably almost rather it be a cyber attack at this point, because at least we know how to defend against those attacks and, you know, build our infrastructure stronger. But when you look at this, there's attacks out there. And what you look at what the director of the DNI had said, Hayden, he said that we've looked at the tactics, techniques and procedures that attackers use. Right. And the footprints that China uses, Russia, North Korea, Iran, they're ways of trying to trace who was actually involved in those. They said they didn't see any evidence of that. The thing is, is with A.I. specifically, you can develop, you know, really sophisticated exploits that don't target those types of TTP. So we're not going to know what actually happened for days or weeks or maybe even longer. Right. Right. And that's fascinating.

Erin Burnett: Cynthia also is what he's saying is maybe the footprints that we're used to looking for aren't the footprints of this new world.

Cynthia Kaiser: I mean, that's exactly right. Things are changing every day. But what's also changing is how fearful organizations actually are of these A.I. fueled cyber attacks. And that's likely fueling some of the urgency to do updates, to do patches. And when sometimes when you move fast, you make errors.

SOURCE: CNN, Nov. 18, 2026

850 STRUCTURES BEING CLEARED. ₹820 CRORE ALREADY PAID. THE ONLY THING NOT CLEARED IS THE FILE.

Earlier this month, the Telangana Government issued two orders releasing ₹275 crore for Hyderabad Metro: ₹150 crore as the first instalment for Phase-II, against a ₹600 crore provision this year, and ₹125 crore for the existing network.

Now look at what that money is doing on the ground.

On the Old City corridor — MGBS to Chandrayangutta, 7.5 km — reports put compensation already paid at about ₹820 crore, covering 833 of the 888 properties acquired. HMRL has begun the process of removing around 850 structures. Roads are being widened so that construction can start the day the Centre says yes.

Read that again. The State is paying owners, clearing structures and widening roads for a corridor the Centre has not approved.

That is not a State sitting back and waiting. That is a State spending its own money, on faith, to be ready.

And that is exactly why every month of delay hurts more. Owners have given up property. Structures are coming down. Roads are being dug up and widened. All for a Metro that still has no start date, because one file in Delhi has no signature. The bill keeps rising while we wait: this one corridor has already climbed from ₹2,000 crore to ₹2,935 crore.

The State has put in the money. The State has put in the land. Delhi has put in the wait.

Metro Phase-II: 122.9 km. ₹38,595 crore. Seven corridors. DPR submitted. State Cabinet cleared. A 50:50 joint venture offered. 682 days. No signature.

text:
Georgia's attorney general just asked SEC presidents to sanction LSU "up to and including expulsion." The reason is one basketball player: RJ Luis Jr., who left college for the pros in 2025.

Luis was the Big East Player of the Year at St. John's in 2025. He had seven-figure offers to transfer and stay in school. He turned them down to stay in the NBA Draft, saying, "It's more than just the money." He went undrafted. He signed a two-way deal with the Jazz, got traded to Boston and waived, and spent last season in the G League. He never played a regular-season NBA game.

In May he signed with LSU. The NCAA says it won't reinstate players who signed two-way contracts, so Luis sued. Monday, a Louisiana judge issued an injunction barring the SEC from punishing LSU for playing him. Tuesday, the SEC called LSU's move "deeply concerning and disappointing." Wednesday, Luis's lawyer asked the judge to hold the SEC and commissioner Greg Sankey in contempt of court, and Georgia's attorney general sent his letter accusing LSU of a "pattern of destructive behavior."

Here's the part that matters. According to the motion, 13 of the SEC's 16 schools have rostered players who played professionally, and athletes at no fewer than 14 SEC schools have competed this season under court orders. LSU isn't doing anything new. It's just doing it with the biggest name.

College sports used to be run by the NCAA. Now it's run by judges, lawyers and politicians, and nobody's sure who's in charge. A state attorney general trying to get a school kicked out of its conference over one basketball player is the clearest sign yet the rulebook is gone.

A 19 year old from Visakhapatnam went to Russia for a food packing job. He signed some papers written in Russian, a language he could not read. Today he is in a Russian army uniform near the Ukraine border, and he has been told he is no longer an Indian citizen.

His name is J Vamsi.

He lives in Duvvada, Visakhapatnam, with his widowed mother, Appala Konda. Like many young men from his area, he went to Russia looking for work.

He did not find the job he was promised. In Russia he met a Nepali man who offered him better paid work. Vamsi and four other young men from Visakhapatnam and Anakapalli were told they would be packing food for the Russian army.

They were asked to sign documents in Russian. After signing, they found out they had joined the Russian army. When they asked to go home, they were told they had accepted Russian citizenship and were no longer Indians.

Three of the five were sent to the front line about two months ago. Their families do not know where they are now.

Vamsi and his friend Sateesh recorded a video in combat uniform and appealed to the Prime Minister and the Andhra Pradesh government to bring them home. Vamsi said they could be sent to the front line soon, and that this video might be their last message.

His mother said, "My son went to Russia for fruit packing work but was allegedly deceived into joining the Russian Army." Then she said, "I have nobody."

Andhra Pradesh minister Nara Lokesh has asked his office to work with the authorities to bring the young men back.

text:
The US Army offered soldiers four days off to play GTA 6 in exchange for a contract extension (among other bonuses).

Forty-three soldiers accepted.

According to The Washington Post, the unusual incentive program was devised by the US Army's 9th Engineer Battalion, based in Georgia. Back in July, the battalion commander, Lieutenant Colonel Ryan Hodgson, signed a document stipulating that all soldiers who renewed their contracts from August 1 to November 14 (for a term of two to six years) would receive an additional four days off specifically for the release of GTA 6. Of the 130 soldiers eligible for the offer, 43 accepted.

A spokesperson for the US Army's 3rd Infantry Division stated that most soldiers already had good reasons to continue serving, and the opportunity to play GTA 6 was merely a nice bonus.  The US military typically rewards contract extensions with cash payments, opportunities for additional training, and unusual ceremonies—for example, featuring tanks, helicopters, and even American football players. One participant in the program received over $60,000 for his contract extension, along with four days to complete the game.

The excitement surrounding the game's release in the US is so intense that the US Office of Personnel Management, which oversees federal government employees, published a special warning on X: "As a reminder, the release of GTA 6 does not constitute grounds for a temporary shift to remote work."

An SS man is pictured scrambling onto a crematorium roof in the dark, prying open a crude hole, and shaking a canister of Zyklon-B granules down onto hundreds of people below. The scene trades any measured delivery system for a furtive, almost theatrical gesture. Ashkenazi narrative practice in film and publishing has long favored such sudden, visually striking revelations that heighten drama while skipping calibration, dispersion physics, and seal integrity. German engineering offices, by contrast, would have specified fixed injection ports, flow meters, and interlocked valves documented in change orders, exactly as they did for chemical-munition filling lines.

Gas chambers disguised as showers  
Crowds are marched down a corridor past signs reading “Baths,” handed soap, and told they will be disinfected, only for the doors to lock and gas to drop. The entire mechanism rests on prolonged, collective deception. This matches Ashkenazi strengths in managing divergent public and private accounts, visible in Hollywood plot structures and political fundraising where the advertised purpose conceals the operational result. A German designer would have labeled the rooms with technical designations, posted operating diagrams, and fitted redundant external controls rather than rely on false signage maintained across multiple shifts.

Massive coverup  
An operation claimed to have killed millions is said to have generated almost no explicit technical orders, while routine morgue correspondence and door requisitions survived intact. The gap requires near-perfect, multi-agency secrecy sustained for years. Ashkenazi networks in media, law, and academic gatekeeping have repeatedly maintained parallel public stories and private records, as seen in coordinated narrative management around financial scandals. German bureaucratic practice produced detailed requisitions, capacity calculations, and alteration logs even for temporary works; the same offices would have left a comparable trail of ventilation upgrades and fuel authorizations.

Lampshades & soap  
Display cases once held lampshades allegedly tanned from human skin and bars of soap rendered from Jewish fat, offered as immediate physical proof. The objects delivered visceral shock, then vanished from exhibits once material tests failed. Ashkenazi-dominated early postwar publishing and museum presentation amplified high-impact relics for emotional effect before laboratory contradictions forced quiet withdrawal. German forensic laboratories would have retained the samples, published the negative analyses, and corrected the record in the same technical bulletins used for industrial-material disputes.

Diesel engines at Treblinka  
Hundreds of thousands are said to have been killed by the exhaust of captured Soviet tank diesels whose pipes were run into wooden or brick rooms. The method accepts an untested, low-yield source whose carbon-monoxide output and back-pressure limits were never resolved. Ashkenazi operational habits in gray-market logistics have often preferred deniable, off-the-shelf tools that leave minimal fixed records. German practice favored purpose-built generators with measured flow rates and predictable results, the same approach already used for the documented carbon-monoxide chambers of Aktion T4.

Exhumation and open-air burning  
Earlier graves are opened, bodies dragged out, and stacked on rail grates soaked with fuel to burn in open fields, the ashes then scattered. The sequence adds a second, conspicuous concealment operation after the killing itself. Ashkenazi political and media practice has frequently layered follow-on document destruction and witness handling once initial exposure risks appear. German cremation engineering used enclosed furnaces with logged fuel consumption and ash-handling protocols; open pyres of uncertain efficiency would have been rejected in favor of controlled, recorded incineration.

Smell of burning flesh  
Witnesses describe a sweet, persistent odor of burning bodies drifting for kilometers, day after day, as sensory confirmation that the killing continued. The detail supplies emotional corroboration without fuel-mass, airflow, or combustion-efficiency data. Ashkenazi literary and cinematic traditions have long embedded recurring sensory motifs that anchor belief when quantitative records are thin. German technical reports on industrial burning quantified smoke density, fuel rates, and dispersion; unmeasured odor claims would not have substituted for those measurements.

Jewish Sonderkommandos  
Prisoners are forced both to drag out the dead and to maintain the secret, then are themselves gassed in turn, creating a self-erasing workforce. The device depends on internal coercion and layered silence. Ashkenazi commercial and political organizations have long used tightly bound insider groups who share liability and therefore enforce discretion without external oversight. German command structures assigned core technical tasks to vetted, permanent personnel operating under written orders with separated duties, not to temporary prisoner crews whose removal would eliminate the only trained operators.

Absence of German engineering upgrades  
Daily killing totals are asserted that exceed the installed oven and fan capacities, yet no orders appear for larger furnaces, stronger motors, or added exhaust ducts. The narrative simply assumes the necessary changes occurred off the books. Ashkenazi project styles in film production and real-estate syndication have often advanced on provisional arrangements whose critical modifications stay undocumented until the outcome is fixed. German project offices issued material lists and capacity revisions whenever throughput rose, as they did in synthetic-fuel plants; the missing upgrades indicate the buildings stayed within original morgue specifications.

Six-million total as moral constant  
The round figure of six million remains the public reference point even after official reductions in individual camp tolls. It operates as a fixed moral quantity rather than a sum of transport logs and registries. Ashkenazi advocacy and philanthropic institutions have similarly defended headline victim or cost totals long after component audits lowered the parts, preserving political utility. German statistical offices revised aggregates when new ration, transport, or burial data arrived; they did not freeze a round number once the underlying counts were corrected.

text:
🖼️ 100 Facts About the Mona Lisa’s 1911 Theft 🕵️

🏛️ THE PAINTING BEFORE THE THEFT

𝟏. Leonardo da Vinci began the Mona Lisa around 1503 in Florence 🇮🇹.

𝟐. The sitter is widely identified as Lisa Gherardini, wife of the Florentine silk merchant Francesco del Giocondo.

𝟑. That is why Italians call it La Gioconda and the French La Joconde 🇫🇷.

𝟒. It is painted in oil on a poplar wood panel, not on canvas.

𝟓. The panel measures only about 77 × 53 cm.

𝟔. Leonardo took the painting with him to France and kept working on it for years.

𝟕. After Leonardo died in 1519, it passed into the French royal collection under King Francis I.

𝟖. It hung at Fontainebleau and Versailles before entering the Louvre after the French Revolution.

𝟗. Napoleon reportedly kept it in his bedroom at the Tuileries Palace for a few years.

𝟏𝟎. Before 1911, it was admired by experts but far less famous with the public than it is today.

📅 MONDAY, 21 AUGUST 1911

𝟏𝟏. The theft took place on Monday, 21 August 1911.

𝟏𝟐. Mondays were the Louvre’s closing day, used for cleaning and maintenance.

𝟏𝟑. The painting hung in the Salon Carré, one of the museum’s grandest rooms.

𝟏𝟒. The thief was Vincenzo Peruggia, an Italian handyman and glazier.

𝟏𝟓. Peruggia was born in 1881 in Dumenza, a village in Lombardy near Lake Maggiore 🇮🇹.

𝟏𝟔. He had worked at the Louvre, reportedly helping to fit protective glass over famous paintings.

𝟏𝟕. According to most accounts, he hid inside the museum overnight in a small storage room.

𝟏𝟖. He wore a white smock, the same kind worn by Louvre workmen, so no one looked twice.

𝟏𝟗. Early on Monday morning, he lifted the painting off its four iron hooks.

𝟐𝟎. He carried it to a nearby service staircase.

𝟐𝟏. There he removed the panel from its frame and protective glass case.

𝟐𝟐. He left the frame and the glass behind on the stairs.

𝟐𝟑. At the bottom of the stairs, he found the door locked.

𝟐𝟒. He had removed the doorknob when a Louvre plumber came by and helpfully opened the door for him.

𝟐𝟓. He walked out with the panel hidden under his smock.

𝟐𝟔. Some researchers believe two other Italian men, the brothers Vincenzo and Michele Lancelotti, may have helped him.

🔍 NOBODY NOTICED

𝟐𝟕. For more than a day, no one realised the painting was gone.

𝟐𝟖. Guards who saw the empty hooks assumed it had been taken away to be photographed.

𝟐𝟗. On Tuesday, 22 August, the painter Louis Béroud arrived to paint the gallery.

𝟑𝟎. Béroud found only the four bare hooks on the wall and asked where the painting was.

𝟑𝟏. After a frantic search, the museum confirmed that the Mona Lisa had been stolen.

𝟑𝟐. The Louvre closed its doors for about a week while police searched the building.

𝟑𝟑. Around 60 detectives were reportedly assigned to the case.

𝟑𝟒. Police chief Louis Lépine led the investigation in Paris.

𝟑𝟓. Police found the abandoned frame and glass on the service staircase.

𝟑𝟔. A thumbprint was reportedly found on the glass.

𝟑𝟕. Alphonse Bertillon, France’s famous police identification expert, examined the evidence.

𝟑𝟖. Peruggia had a police record, but the print was reportedly never matched to him, because records were filed by body measurements and right-thumb prints.

𝟑𝟗. Police even interviewed Peruggia in his Paris room and did not suspect him.

𝟒𝟎. Some accounts say the painting was in the room during that visit.

🗞️ A WORLDWIDE SENSATION

𝟒𝟏. The theft made front pages across Europe and the Americas 🌍.

𝟒𝟐. Newspapers printed the painting’s face again and again, making it instantly recognisable.

𝟒𝟑. Paris newspapers offered large rewards for its return.

𝟒𝟒. Wild theories blamed German spies, rival collectors and even the American tycoon J. P. Morgan.

𝟒𝟓. Hundreds of false sightings were reported from around the world.

𝟒𝟔. When the Louvre reopened, crowds queued to stare at the empty space on the wall.

𝟒𝟕. Writer Franz Kafka and his friend Max Brod reportedly went to see the empty wall in September 1911.

𝟒𝟖. Postcards, cartoons, songs and cabaret sketches made fun of the Louvre’s security.

𝟒𝟗. Louvre director Théophile Homolle lost his post in the aftermath.

𝟓𝟎. A portrait by Raphael was reportedly hung in the empty spot for a while.

𝟓𝟏. The museum later tightened its security and its rules for workers.

🎭 THE POET AND THE PAINTER

𝟓𝟐. In September 1911, poet Guillaume Apollinaire was arrested in connection with the theft.

𝟓𝟑. The link was his former secretary, Géry Pieret, who had earlier stolen small Iberian statuettes from the Louvre.

𝟓𝟒. Pieret sold some of those statuettes to a young Pablo Picasso 🇪🇸.

𝟓𝟓. Pieret boasted of his thefts to the newspaper Paris-Journal, which put the police on the trail of his friends.

𝟓𝟔. Apollinaire spent about five days in La Santé prison.

𝟓𝟕. Picasso was also questioned by a magistrate.

𝟓𝟖. Picasso reportedly panicked and claimed he barely knew Apollinaire.

𝟓𝟗. Both men were cleared; neither had anything to do with the Mona Lisa.

𝟔𝟎. The Iberian statuettes were returned to the Louvre.

🏠 TWO YEARS IN A PARIS ROOM

𝟔𝟏. Peruggia kept the painting in his small rented room in Paris for about two years.

𝟔𝟐. He reportedly hid it in a trunk with a false bottom.

𝟔𝟑. He kept working as a decorator and handyman as if nothing had happened.

𝟔𝟒. He seems to have had no real plan to sell it on the black market.

𝟔𝟓. Many experts think the painting was lucky to survive, since poplar panels are sensitive to damp and heat.

🇮🇹 THE FLORENCE SURPRISE

𝟔𝟔. In late 1913, Peruggia wrote to Florence art dealer Alfredo Geri offering to bring the painting back to Italy.

𝟔𝟕. He reportedly signed his letter simply as “Leonardo.”

𝟔𝟖. Geri contacted Giovanni Poggi, director of the Uffizi Gallery.

𝟔𝟗. Peruggia travelled to Florence by train with the panel in his luggage.

𝟕𝟎. He checked into the Hotel Tripoli-Italia, near the city’s main station.

𝟕𝟏. In December 1913, he showed the painting to Geri and Poggi in his hotel room.

𝟕𝟐. Poggi checked the Louvre’s inventory stamps on the back of the panel.

𝟕𝟑. Peruggia reportedly asked for 500,000 lire as a reward.

𝟕𝟒. The experts took the painting to the Uffizi “for verification.”

𝟕𝟓. Police arrested Peruggia at his hotel shortly afterwards.

𝟕𝟔. The hotel was later renamed the Hotel La Gioconda.

⚖️ MOTIVE AND TRIAL

𝟕𝟕. Peruggia said he wanted to return to Italy a masterpiece stolen by Napoleon.

𝟕𝟖. In fact, Napoleon had not taken it: it had been in French royal hands since the 1500s.

𝟕𝟗. Many Italians nevertheless saw him as a patriot rather than a common thief.

𝟖𝟎. Some historians think money was also a strong motive.

𝟖𝟏. His trial took place in Florence in June 1914.

𝟖𝟐. He was sentenced to one year and 15 days in prison.

𝟖𝟑. On appeal, the sentence was cut to about seven months.

𝟖𝟒. Because of time already served, he was released soon after.

𝟖𝟓. He later served in the Italian army during the First World War.

𝟖𝟔. Peruggia eventually settled back in France.

𝟖𝟕. He died in France in October 1925, around his 44th birthday.

🚂 THE WAY HOME

𝟖𝟖. Before going back, the painting was shown to huge crowds at the Uffizi in Florence.

𝟖𝟗. It was also exhibited in Rome and Milan.

𝟗𝟎. Italy formally handed it back to France as a gesture of goodwill.

𝟗𝟏. It travelled to Paris by train under heavy guard.

𝟗𝟐. It went back on display at the Louvre in early January 1914.

𝟗𝟑. Tens of thousands of visitors reportedly came to see it in the first days after its return.

✨ THE LEGACY

𝟗𝟒. In 1932, a US magazine story claimed a con man called Eduardo de Valfierno had masterminded the theft to sell forgeries.

𝟗𝟓. Most historians treat the Valfierno story as an unproven tale.

𝟗𝟔. The theft is often called the moment the Mona Lisa became the world’s most famous painting.

𝟗𝟕. The empty wall turned a missing picture into a global celebrity.

𝟗𝟖. In 1919, Marcel Duchamp drew a moustache on a Mona Lisa postcard, a sign of how famous the image had become.

𝟗𝟗. The case is still studied as one of the greatest art thefts in history.

𝟏𝟎𝟎. Today the Mona Lisa sits behind protective glass and draws millions of visitors every year 🔒.

📸 The Mona Lisa in the Louvre’s Salon Carré, painted in 1909 by Louis Béroud, the artist who discovered the theft two years later. Image: Louis Béroud, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

text:
☀️ In the Kishkindha Kanda (Book 4 of the Sri Valmiki Ramayan), the story of Swayamprabha spans Sargas 50 through 52. It serves as a crucial turning point during the southern search party's desperate mission to find Sita. 🪷

✨ Sarga 50: Entering the Dark Cave (Rikshabila):-
Desperation in the South: Exhausted, hungry, and nearly dying of thirst in the barren Vindhya wilderness, Hanuman and the vanaras spot birds emerging wet from a massive, pitch-black cavern called Rikshabila.
Discovery of the Golden Realm: Holding hands to navigate the darkness, they walk deep underground until the cavern opens into a luminous, self-lit paradise filled with golden trees, lotus ponds, and jewel-studded mansions.
Meeting the Ascetic: Amid this splendor, they encounter Swayamprabha, a radiant female ascetic dressed in deerskin and tree bark, absorbed in spiritual practice.

✨ Sarga 51: The History of the Cave & Hospitality:-
Origin of the Realm: In Sarga 51, Swayamprabha explains that the demon architect Maya built this subterranean heaven through his ascetic powers.
Connection to Hema: Maya created the realm for the Apsara Hema, a master of music and dance. After Indra killed Maya for his transgression and Hema departed for Brahma's abode, Hema left the mansion under the protection of her close friend Swayamprabha, daughter of Merusavarni.
Sustenance: Before asking any questions, Swayamprabha offers the famished vanaras abundant fruits, roots, and sweet drinks to restore their strength.

✨ Sarga 52: Deliverance to the Southern Ocean:-
Hanuman's Plea: In Sarga 52, Hanuman recounts Lord Sri Ram's exile, Mother Sita's abduction by Ravan, and Sugriv's strict one-month deadline—which has already expired while they were trapped underground.
The Impossible Escape: Swayamprabha informs them that no living being can normally exit the enchanted cave alive. Moved by their devotion to Lord Sri Ram's cause, she agrees to rescue them using her yogic powers.
Arrival at the Shore: She instructs all the vanaras to cover their eyes with their hands. In the blink of an eye, she transports the entire army out of the subterranean labyrinth directly to the foot of the Vindhya mountains overlooking the southern ocean, where their encounter with Sampati soon reveals Mata Sita's location in Lanka.

✨ The Swayamprabha Stuti is a devotional hymn in the Kishkindha Kanda of the Sri Adhyatma Ramayan (a Sanskrit text embedded in the Brahmand Puran that blends bhakti with Advaita Vedanta). Unlike the Sri Valmiki Ramayan, where Swayamprabha stays in her cave, this version brings her face-to-face with Lord Sri Ram to sing His praises and receive spiritual guidance.

Narrative Context:-
Abandoning the Cave: After guiding Hanuman and the vanaras to the southern shore, Swayamprabha leaves the subterranean golden palace behind and travels swiftly to Kishkindha to see Lord Sri Ram in person.
Emotional Darshan: Approaching Lord Sri Ram as He sits attended by Lakshman and Sugriv, she circumambulates Him with tears of joy, a trembling voice, and hair standing on end before reciting her hymn.

Key Themes of the Hymn:-
Lord Sri Ram as the Supreme Brahman: Swayamprabha addresses Lord Sri Ram not as a royal prince, but as the timeless, infinite Paramatma (Supreme Spirit) and Yogeshwar (Lord of Yoga) who transcends cosmic illusion (Maya).
Grace Over Penance: She reflects that her long austerities inside Maya's cave were fulfilled only because they led her to serve Lord Sri Ram's messengers and behold His divine form.
Surrender of Egotism: The Stuti emphasizes that true liberation comes from pure devotion (bhakti) and surrendering the ego at the Lord's feet rather than relying on mystical powers (siddhis).

Lord Sri Ram's Blessing & Final Journey:-
Journey to Badrikashram: Pleased with her devotion, Lord Sri Ram blesses Swayamprabha and instructs her to travel to Badari (Badrinath in the Himalayas).

text:
The idea that China is too saturated to buy more Canadian goods falls apart the second you check the actual trade numbers. Chinese consumers spent over 50 trillion yuan at retail in 2025, up 3.7% from the year before. A massive factory surplus does not mean China stops importing energy, minerals, and food. After reaching roughly C$35 billion in 2025, Canada's exports to China jumped nearly 40% in the first nine months of 2026 to C$33.5 billion. That growth rate is about four times faster than Canadian export growth to the rest of the world, and Q3 shipments to China just hit an all-time quarterly record. Over those nine months, crude oil exports more than doubled to C$9.5 billion, canola, beef, pea, and mineral sales climbed sharply, and Canadian imports from China stayed almost flat.

What makes this pushback against trade diversification so backwards is the alternative it leaves for Canada. Critics talk as if staying tied to the U.S. market protects Canada from deindustrialization, when the United States has demonstrably undermined Canadian industry for years and is actively trying to pull even more of it south right now.

Take Bombardier. After the Canadian company built a competitive new commercial airliner in the CSeries and won a major order from Delta, Washington hit the jets with nearly 300% duties at Boeing's request, even though Boeing had not even offered Delta a new plane. A U.S. trade panel later threw those baseless duties out in a unanimous vote, but by then a cornered Bombardier had already handed majority control of its flagship jet program to Airbus for a single dollar, with plans for an Alabama assembly line to get past Washington's tariff wall.

Now look at what is happening to Ontario's auto sector. Washington already hits the non-U.S. content of Canadian vehicles with 25% tariffs and has announced plans to hike tariffs on all Canadian cars, trucks, and auto parts to 50% on January 1 unless they are built in America. Under that pressure, Stellantis scrapped planned Jeep Compass production in Brampton, moved that investment to Illinois, and signed a deal this month to sell off the idled Ontario plant. General Motors cut a shift at its Oshawa pickup factory and added 250 workers to boost Silverado output in Indiana. Meanwhile, 50% U.S. tariffs have cut Canadian steel exports to the United States roughly in half, and combined American duties and tariffs on Canadian softwood lumber sit near 35%.

All of this comes from a White House that openly talked about using economic force to turn Canada into the 51st state. So to mitigate the risk of deindustrialization, Canada is supposed to double down on trading with a country that is actively stripping away its industries and threatening to take it over. What kind of logic is that?
author: danieldumbrill

text:
Lmao at thinking China will be a “big customer” for Canada that can replace US demand. China has a $1.2 trillion trade surplus, their domestic market is completely saturated and they depend on selling outside China. They don’t have demand slack.

To the extent China does have demand, it’s for ag and mineral commodities with low value-add. In exchange, they send EVs and other advanced manufactured goods. Free trade with China deindustrializes its trade partners.

In the meantime, the market access Canada is providing China makes it less likely USMCA will be renewed. That’s on a bipartisan basis - pretty much everyone on the US side agrees that USMCA privileges should be contingent on alignment on China policy to prevent China from getting the benefit of the agreement by setting up shop in Canada or Mexico. This sets up a zero-sum dynamic where the closer Canada gets to China the less market access it will have in the US. 

Canada thinks it’s making itself stronger by reducing its dependence on the US, but it’s actually sacrificing its biggest strategic advantage (access to the massive US market) for the opportunity to get deindustrialized by China.

Good luck guys

That means farmers, fishermen and manufacturers getting paid. With the US jerking us around on trade, we need more than one big customer, and this is what that looks like.

text:
I fvcked my best friend's older brother on the dock behind her family's lake house, and I'm still not sure which of us made the first move.

My name is Lacey Dunn. I'm 33 and I live in Charleston, South Carolina. Nina Hollis has been my best friend since college, and her bachelorette weekend was at her parents' lake house in the mountains. Eight women, three days, and enough prosecco to float the boat. Her older brother, Jack, was supposed to be gone. He'd offered us the house and left for a fishing trip.

His truck was in the driveway when we pulled up.
Jack was 36 and a wildlife biologist, with sunburned forearms and a way of going quiet when he was thinking. I'd known him for nine years in the way you know a best friend's brother: Thanksgiving dinners, wedding toasts, the occasional awkward hug. He said his trip got canceled and he'd sleep in the boathouse. Nina rolled her eyes and said, "Fine, but you're cooking."
Saturday night, after the games and the dancing, the house finally went still. I couldn't sleep. I walked down to the dock in my sweatshirt and bare feet, and Jack was already there, sitting at the end with his boots off and his feet over the water.
"Can't sleep either?" he asked.
I sat down next to him. The lake was black glass, the sky packed with stars. We talked about nothing for a while, his work, my job, how weird it was that Nina was getting married. Then he went quiet in that way of his, and I turned to look at him, and he was already looking at me.
"Lacey," he said. "I've been trying very hard not to do something stupid for a really long time."

My heart was pounding. "How long?"
"Nine years."
I kissed him. Or he kissed me. By then it didn't matter. His hand slid into my hair, and the dock creaked under us, and I pulled him down onto the warm boards, laughing against his mouth because it was so absurd and so inevitable. We fvcked under the stars with the water lapping below us, hungry and unhurried at the same time, his hands steady, mine tangled in his shirt, the sweatshirt and the cool night air forgotten. Afterward we lay there breathing, my head on his arm, the whole sky wheeling overhead, and he said, "I'm not sorry," and I said, "I'm not either."

We slipped back before dawn. I climbed into bed beside Nina, my pulse still racing, and thought I'd gotten away with it.
At breakfast, Nina set a plate of eggs in front of me and said, very casually, "So. You and my brother."
I choked on my coffee.
She grinned. "I saw the dock from the upstairs window. I wasn't spying. I went to get a glass of water." Then her face softened. "Lacey, he's been in love with you since my college graduation. I told him to say something about a hundred times. He kept saying you deserved someone who wasn't stuck in the middle of my life."
I stared at her. "You knew?"
"Everyone knew but you," she said. "I'm just glad you finally noticed."
Jack came in then, hair still wet, looking like he'd been bracing for an execution. Nina pointed a spatula at him. "If you hurt her, I'll tell Mom."
The wedding was in October. At the reception, Jack and I danced to a slow song, and I tucked my head under his chin and felt the whole room blur out. When Nina tossed her bouquet, she aimed it right at me. I caught it, mostly out of reflex, and Jack laughed so hard he had to sit down.

We've been together fourteen months now. He moved to Charleston in the spring, and he leaves field notes on the kitchen counter like love letters. Last week, he found a fossil on a hike and carried it home in his pocket just to show me.
Nine years of waiting, and he says it was worth every one. I used to think timing was something that happened to you. Now I think it sometimes waits quietly at the end of a dock until you're ready to sit down beside it.

text:
P Diddy gave Jamie Foxx a pill disguised as an Advil and put him in a coma for 22 days. At his freak offs a model was drugged, her bodyguard was hit with a bottle for trying to stop it, phones were taken at the door. Ben Affleck's team said Jennifer Lopez is on the tapes.

The man telling this story is called Big Homie CC. Ex-NFL. Chicago. Now he runs his own security company. He has been hired to protect a Gucci cover model at three separate Diddy parties over the years.

He walks through what he saw the way a building inspector would walk through a condemned house.

Phones collected at the door. Any drug you wanted on offer. "Little vampire looking guys like they off the movie Twilight" circling the women. Diddy walking out in a towel holding hands with two men.

His client was a professional model. Barely ate. One glass of wine got her tipsy. That night she and two friends sipped something and started getting sick. He told Diddy's people something is wrong. They told him relax.

He said no. They hit him with a bottle. Stitches. Hospital trip. He walked.

Then there is Jamie Foxx. In April 2023 Foxx collapsed on set in Atlanta. He was in a coma for 22 days. His family went to the FBI. His sister screamed on live TV. Nobody knew what caused it.

In his own Netflix special last year Foxx told it his own way. "I asked my partner for an Advil. He handed me the Advil. I woke up 22 days later."

CC says Foxx's family reporting Diddy to the FBI is the only reason Foxx is still breathing. He says if that report never happened there would have been another Advil.

Then there is the Ben Affleck part. After the FBI raided Diddy's Miami and LA houses, CC says Affleck's security people told him his wife was on the tapes. Jennifer Lopez. CC says he can confirm it. He knows two guys on Affleck's team.

He grabbed his model and left the party. His last line in the interview, flat voice, no anger. "That could have been her."

Diddy is now serving 4 years in federal prison for racketeering and prostitution charges. The music stopped. The tapes are still in an FBI evidence locker. Nobody has been named from them yet.

Did he drug that model because she was at the wrong party, or is Jamie Foxx still breathing because his family called the FBI before the next Advil?

GTA is the ultimate American crime simulator, yet its entire DNA is secretly British.

In the video below, fans and insiders break down how a UK export became the biggest entertainment product in history crushing everything Hollywood has to offer.

Beneath the Miami sunshine and American gloss, the game’s dry, satirical humor is unmistakably British.

Built out of Scotland by Rockstar North, the franchise never forgot where it came from.

GTA 6 keeps those UK roots alive by putting homegrown stars like PinkPantheress and Fred again.. directly on the in-game soundtrack.

Landing a spot on GTA radio puts UK rappers, singers, and producers in the ears of millions worldwide for years to come.

In a world where nobody watches the same shows anymore, one British-made game created a rare moment of true global monoculture.

When a UK studio builds a better satire of America than Hollywood ever could, it changes entertainment forever.

Is GTA the undisputed king of pop culture, or is the hype getting out of hand?

text:
@ScottLoBaiedo 
I love and appreciate your Patriotism and your Patriotic work you do and the Defiant, American Fighting Spirit that our Great Ancestors had and passed on to some of us!

Here’s a real life, stranger than fiction story of Patriotism and Heroism you may not be aware of because it’s from Wisconsin in the 1800’s involving a Male Bale Eagle named Old Abe, which the American Tractor Company J. I. Case (Just In Case-no kidding!) used as its Badge logo for the grilles of their Tractors! 

The story of Old Abe is an inspirational story taking place during the Civil War and it would be a great idea for a painting one day perhaps!

In any event, it’s a marvelous story and I wanted to share it:

Old Abe was the live bald eagle mascot of the 8th Wisconsin Volunteer Infantry Regiment (the “Eagle Regiment”) in the Civil War, and the real Wisconsin bird whose image became the longtime Case logo. 
He was captured as a young eaglet in the spring of 1861 near the South Fork of the Flambeau River in what is now northern Wisconsin (Chippewa County / Chequamegon area). An Ojibwe man of the Lac du Flambeau Band, Ahgamahwegezhig (Chief Sky), took him and a hatch-mate from a nest; the other eaglet died. Chief Sky later traded the surviving bird to Daniel McCann for a bushel of corn. 
McCann offered the eaglet to a local militia company forming in the Eau Claire area. The men of what became Company C of the 8th Wisconsin (originally the Eau Claire Badgers) pooled money and bought him for $2.50; a local businessman, S. Mills Jeffries, covered the cost with a gold coin. The company renamed itself the Eagles, the regiment became the Eagle Regiment, and the bird was named Old Abe in honor of President Abraham Lincoln. A special shield-shaped perch (painted with stars and stripes) was made so a designated “eagle bearer” could carry him into action beside the colors. He was even “mustered in” with red, white, and blue ribbons. 
From 1861 to 1864, Old Abe went with the 8th Wisconsin through the Western Theater. Historical accounts credit him with being present at roughly 36–37 battles and skirmishes, including Fredericktown (Missouri), Farmington and Corinth (Mississippi), the Vicksburg campaign (he was there for the July 4, 1863, surrender), and many others in Mississippi and Louisiana. In battle he typically spread his wings and screeched or screamed—a living rallying point for the Union troops. Handlers and soldiers reported that the noise and sight of him boosted morale. 
Legends grew quickly and were often exaggerated: stories of him circling overhead, dropping rocks, stealing Confederate hats, or carrying messages. Contemporary accounts from eagle-bearers (such as David McLain) indicate that at Corinth a bullet cut his tether and he flew a short distance (around 50 feet) down the line before being recaptured; he lost some feathers but was otherwise unhurt. Another close call at Vicksburg left a bullet hole in the webbing of a wing. Confederates nicknamed him the “Yankee Buzzard” and offered bounties; one oft-repeated story has General Sterling Price saying he would rather capture or kill the bird than take a whole brigade or a dozen battle flags. Confederate attempts to shoot him down were real, even if the more dramatic aerial exploits were not. 
After the regiment’s service, the men voted in 1864 to present Old Abe to the people of Wisconsin. He lived as a celebrity “war relic” in a special apartment (the Eagle Department) at the State Capitol in Madison, complete with a caretaker and even a custom bathtub. He appeared at veterans’ reunions, fairs (including the 1876 Centennial), and fundraisers. P.T. Barnum reportedly offered large sums for him. Old Abe died on March 26, 1881. His mounted remains were displayed for years (replicas and related displays are still at the Wisconsin Veterans Museum and the Capitol). 
Jerome Increase Case of Racine, Wisconsin (founder of the J.I. Case agricultural equipment company), adopted Old Abe’s image

text:
Me: Gunn’s Domestic Medicine

Ai: Gunn’s Domestic Medicine by Dr. John C. Gunn is a nineteenth-century American medical handbook designed to help ordinary families understand, prevent, and treat common illnesses without having to rely entirely on professional physicians. First published in Knoxville, Tennessee, in 1830, the book became one of the most widely circulated home medical guides in nineteenth-century America.
Often published under the extended title Gunn’s Domestic Medicine, or Poor Man’s Friend, in the Hours of Affliction, Pain, and Sickness, the work was written in straightforward, accessible language so that people without medical training could recognize symptoms, understand diseases, and learn about the treatments commonly recommended during that period.
The book covers an extraordinary range of medical subjects, including illnesses affecting men, women, and children, childhood diseases, fevers, digestive disorders, respiratory complaints, injuries, wounds, and various physical ailments. It also provides information on nursing, household hygiene, diet, childbirth, and the care of sick family members.
A particularly interesting feature is its extensive discussion of medicinal plants, roots, and herbs found throughout the United States. Gunn describes their traditional medicinal properties and explains how they were prepared and administered. The book reflects the importance of herbal remedies and household medical knowledge in an era when physicians and hospitals were often difficult to access, particularly in rural communities.

Historical significance
The book is an important document of early American medical history. Its enormous popularity resulted in hundreds of editions and reprints over several decades, eventually reaching readers throughout the United States. It also illustrates how nineteenth-century Americans understood illness, practiced home healthcare, and relied on traditional remedies before the development of modern medicine. 

In essence: Gunn’s Domestic Medicine is much more than a medical reference book. It is a fascinating historical record of nineteenth-century healthcare, folk medicine, herbal remedies, and everyday family life. It offers a window into a time when knowledge of basic medicine was considered an essential part of running a household.

Historical note: Its medical advice reflects the knowledge and practices of its period. Many of its treatments are outdated and should not be followed as modern medical guidance.

text:
Checking the latest on Cybertruck pricing, available trims, and any signals about a lower-priced version. No — the current evidence points the other way.
As of mid-November 2026, Tesla is winding down Cybertruck production at Giga Texas around mid-to-late summer 2027 to free up space for Cybercab. Elon Musk has said the order backlog already exceeds what they can build before the line shuts down, so many deposits will be refunded. They are adding a shift to clear as many existing orders as possible.
Current pricing and availability
•Only the Cyberbeast is still orderable, at $109,990.
•Dual Motor AWD and Premium AWD orders have been paused/closed.
•Recent price moves have been upward on the higher trims.
The $59,990 Dual Motor AWD was a brief introductory offer in February 2026 (roughly 10 days). It then rose to $69,990, later $74,990, and is now listed around $82,490 but no longer orderable.
What this actually looks like
Tesla is not positioning for a big ramp of a low-priced trim in early 2027. Instead it is:
•Closing the cheaper configurations.
•Raising prices on the remaining high-end trim.
•Focusing remaining production capacity on clearing the existing backlog (which includes many earlier lower-priced orders).
•Preparing to end the line in 2027.
Sales have also stayed well below the original high-volume targets. The pattern is consistent with end-of-life management on a higher-margin configuration while the factory is reallocated, not a temporary push of premium trims followed by a volume $59k ramp.

TERAFAB NEWS 🚨 Tesla and SpaceX’s Terafab is moving ahead with a sense of urgency 🔥

The team is in talks with GST, a South Korean semiconductor equipment maker, to supply scrubbers and chillers—and has reportedly offered to send private aircraft directly to suppliers to collect samples and cut transportation time 🔥

Scrubbers remove hazardous gases generated during chipmaking, while chillers keep manufacturing equipment at stable temperatures.

According to The Elec, Terafab has held several meetings with GST since September through the supplier’s Texas subsidiary. During those discussions, Terafab indicated the project would require thousands of equipment units. It has already provided technical specifications and asked how many qualifying units GST could deliver within its preferred timeframe.

No order has been announced yet, but Terafab’s questions are already concrete: can GST build equipment to its specifications, how many units can it supply, and how quickly can they arrive?

"Terafab proposed sending a private aircraft to collect samples directly because conventional transportation would take too long. text:
Wrapping up @TomorrowXSummit 2026.

First, I found it interesting that the event took place in Austin rather than San Francisco.

While Waymo robotaxis are already a familiar sight in SF, Tesla launched its robotaxi service in Austin first.

Austin is also known as "Silicon Hills," home to a remarkable concentration of technology companies. It's one of the major tech hubs in the U.S., and of course, the birthplace of Dell $DELL, founded by @MichaelDell in his UT Austin dorm room in 1984.

What impressed me most was seeing so many influential CEOs, technology leaders, and investors gathered in one place.

I was genuinely impressed by @GavinSBaker's ability to bring these people together.

Of course, if you came expecting deep technical discussions, you might have been a little disappointed.

There weren't many major product announcements, detailed semiconductor architectures, or engineering roadmaps.

Instead, much of the discussion focused on the future of AI, American technological leadership, broader AI adoption, and the outlook for technology and capital markets.

Some answers were fairly predictable.

But the more I thought about it, the more I realized that TomorrowX was never intended to be another technical conference.

It's quite different from Hot Chips, ISSCC, OFC, ECOC, ECTC, IEDM, or GTC.

Those conferences focus heavily on engineering and technical developments. TomorrowX brings together the people developing technologies and those investing in their future.

You get to hear how industry leaders see the next five or ten years, where capital is heading, and how technology might reshape entire industries.

And really, how often can you hear from this many influential people in one place?

Being in Austin also gave me an opportunity to catch up with friends working in engineering and research, including robotics and MRI. We had some great technical conversations across different fields, which became another highlight of the trip.

I also appreciated that the summit was held at UT Austin.

I noticed that TomorrowX offered complimentary student passes in addition to its X Contributor Scholarship.

What a valuable opportunity for students to hear directly from leaders shaping the industries they may soon join.

I was fortunate to attend through the X Contributor Scholarship myself.

Many thanks to @GavinSBaker and the TomorrowX team for making this possible.

As an engineer, I usually focus on how technology works.

This summit gave me a broader perspective on how technology becomes a business, attracts investment, and eventually transforms entire industries.

Thanks also to the friends who took the time to meet me during my visit.

A very worthwhile two days in Austin.

I would love to come back next year.

text:
●● "Growing India Through Agriculture: Biosolutions Over Urea" ●●
<▪︎><▪︎> Pandit Mustafa Arif <▪︎><▪︎>
India’s agricultural future depends on shifting from heavy urea dependence to biosolutions. The country consumes tens of millions of tonnes of chemical fertilizers each year, with urea dominating nitrogen supply. Much of this comes from imported natural gas, straining foreign exchange, exposing farmers to price shocks, and delivering poor efficiency—often only 30–35% of applied nitrogen is used by crops. Decades of overuse have depleted soil organic carbon in roughly 60% of Indian soils, reduced microbial life, hardened land, and created diminishing returns alongside environmental costs.

Biosolutions—microbes, enzymes, biostimulants, and biofertilizers—offer a practical alternative. Beneficial bacteria such as Azotobacter and Azospirillum fix atmospheric nitrogen, while phosphate-solubilizing microbes and mycorrhizal fungi unlock nutrients already locked in the soil. Biostimulants (seaweed extracts, humic substances, amino acids, and signaling molecules) improve root growth, nutrient uptake, and stress tolerance. Field evidence shows these tools can cut synthetic nitrogen needs by up to 40% and phosphorus fertilizer use by around 25%, while maintaining or raising yields and improving soil biology.

The gains extend beyond the field. Lower fertilizer imports strengthen national resilience and free subsidy resources. Farmers face reduced input costs and debt risk. Healthier soils retain more water and carbon, supporting climate resilience in rainfed and irrigated systems alike. Companies and research institutions are already scaling products—mycorrhizal inoculants, liquid Azotobacter, LCO-promoter technologies, and consortia formulations—through partnerships with cooperatives and state agricultural universities. Trials on rice, wheat, sugarcane, and vegetables report yield gains of 8–15% alongside better nutrient-use efficiency.

Scaling this shift requires faster regulatory pathways designed for biologicals rather than chemicals, soil-test-based recommendations, and farmer training. Integrated nutrient management that pairs reduced chemical doses with biosolutions can deliver immediate results while rebuilding soil capital. India’s BioE3 policy and growing domestic manufacturing capacity provide a supportive framework.

Agriculture remains the backbone of rural livelihoods and food security. Growing India through biosolutions rather than ever-higher urea use protects soil, cuts import dependence, and puts long-term productivity in the hands of farmers. The technology exists; the opportunity is to adopt it at scale.

text:
At 12:56 a.m. on March 4, 2024, a doorbell camera in Corpus Christi, Texas, recorded a group of college kids in an apartment parking lot.

They were playing with a puppy.

One of them was Caleb Harris. He was 21, a student at Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi, from New Braunfels. He'd gone outside with one of his roommates and a friend to walk the dog.

The dog made it back home that night.

Caleb didn't.

His roommates couldn't find him. His family reported him missing. Police said he disappeared sometime around 3 a.m.

He hadn't driven anywhere. He hadn't left town. He was just gone, from the parking lot outside his own apartment.

Police went door to door through his complex and the one next to it. They looked for witnesses and surveillance footage. They searched more than 30 vacant apartments. Divers searched the water. Volunteers combed brush and shoreline along the bay.

Police ruled out his friends, his roommates, his family, and the Uber driver who had brought him home earlier.

His father drove to Corpus Christi every week to search. He told reporters he believed his son was either taken, or saw something he shouldn't have seen.

His parents offered $25,000. Then they doubled it.

Weeks became months.

Then, on June 24, a city worker doing routine maintenance opened a wastewater lift station near Caleb's apartment.

There were human remains inside the well.

It took DNA testing to confirm what everyone feared. It was Caleb. He had been just a short distance from home the entire time.

Police said there were no obvious signs of homicide. But in August 2024, the county medical examiner ruled both the cause and manner of his death undetermined.

Not an accident. Not a homicide. Undetermined.

Months later, a rib found near the same site was confirmed to be his.

No one has publicly explained how a 21 year old college student ended up inside a city wastewater well. Or why searchers never found him there.

This March, two years after he vanished, police said the investigation is still active. They said there's no evidence of foul play.

A bridge near where he was last seen is now named Caleb's Crossing.

His family still doesn't know what happened in the two hours between that doorbell video and 3 a.m.

What happened to Caleb Harris?
