text:
A bit more on Grant as - "The Steadfast Center" (in Sheridan's words) of Union Grand Strategy. Seriously, can any one deny he was a great general?  

The true measure of Ulysses S. Grant's greatness as a general lies not merely in the battles he won, the territory he captured, or the Confederate armies he compelled to surrender. It lies in something larger: his ability to conceive of the Civil War as a single, interconnected struggle and to make the widely separated armies of the Union serve one common strategic purpose. Grant was not simply a successful field commander. He was a grand strategist, and in the final years of the war he became the organizing intelligence behind the Union's military effort.

The transformation began with the great victories of 1863. The capture of Vicksburg on July 4 severed the Confederacy along the Mississippi River. The trans-Mississippi states were effectively cut off from the eastern Confederacy, making the movement of men, supplies, and matériel across the river extraordinarily difficult. The victory was more than the capture of a fortified city. It altered the geographical and logistical structure of the war.

A few months later, the victories at Chattanooga, including Lookout Mountain and Missionary Ridge, opened the gateway into Georgia and broke the Confederate hold on much of Tennessee. The Union now possessed a powerful position from which to advance into the Confederate interior. These victories were complementary. Vicksburg had divided the Confederacy along the Mississippi; Chattanooga threatened its vital railway connections and opened the route into the heart of the Deep South.

Grant understood the cumulative significance of these developments. He saw that the Confederacy could not be defeated merely by winning isolated battles or capturing strategically important cities. Its armies, transportation networks, industrial resources, communications, and capacity to sustain resistance had to be attacked as parts of a single system. The war had to be prosecuted everywhere, not episodically, and the Union's superior resources had to be brought to bear in a coordinated fashion.

His elevation to command of all Union armies in March 1864 provided the opportunity to put that conception into practice.

Grant's instructions to General George Meade on April 9, 1864, contain perhaps the clearest statement of his strategic philosophy:

"So far as practicable, all the armies are to move together and toward one common center."

The sentence is deceptively simple. Behind it lay a comprehensive plan involving Meade against Lee in Virginia, Butler operating against Richmond from the south, Sherman moving against Joseph E. Johnston and into Georgia, Banks concentrating against Mobile, and Union forces in West Virginia threatening Confederate communications and railroads. The details would change, and not every part of the plan would succeed. Banks's projected operation against Mobile, for example, did not unfold as Grant intended. But the governing conception was unmistakable: the Confederate armies were not to be permitted to reinforce one another at will while Union armies operated independently and gave the enemy opportunities to concentrate against them one at a time.

Grant intended to deny the Confederacy that freedom of movement. If Lee were pressed in Virginia, Johnston would be pressed in Georgia. If Confederate forces attempted to reinforce one theater, they would expose another. The Union armies would exert simultaneous pressure, compelling the Confederacy to defend an increasingly untenable position on multiple fronts.

Sherman's role was central to this design. Grant identified Johnston's army as his immediate objective and the "heart of Georgia as his ultimate aim." Sherman was to break Johnston's capacity to resist, penetrate the Confederate interior, and damage the resources that sustained the war. In practical terms, this meant that Sherman would be exerting pressure on the Confederate rear while Grant confronted Lee in Virginia. The armies were separated geographically, but their operations were strategically connected.

It is important to distinguish Grant's strategic conception from the precise operational plan Sherman later devised. Grant did not lay out the March to the Sea in April 1864. That particular march emerged after Atlanta fell, when Sherman proposed moving through Georgia to the coast. Grant approved it. The distinction does not diminish Grant's achievement. On the contrary, it illustrates one of his greatest qualities: he established the strategic objectives and gave capable subordinates considerable latitude in determining how best to accomplish them.

The campaign against Atlanta demonstrated the effectiveness of that relationship. Sherman kept Johnston's army under relentless pressure, eventually forced its retreat, and captured Atlanta in September 1864. The city was a major railway junction, industrial center, and supply depot. Its loss was a serious blow to the Confederacy and a tremendous political victory for Lincoln. It also helped prevent Confederate forces in Georgia from being freely transferred to Lee in Virginia. The subsequent march through Georgia extended Union power deep into the Confederate interior, disrupted transportation and supplies, and demonstrated how vulnerable the Confederacy had become.

Meanwhile, Grant personally accompanied the Army of the Potomac in the campaign against Lee. The Wilderness, Spotsylvania, North Anna, and Cold Harbor were among the bloodiest engagements of the war. Lee possessed the advantages of familiar terrain, interior lines, and the ability to concentrate his forces at threatened points. Grant suffered enormous casualties, and his critics fastened upon the losses as evidence of unimaginative butchery.

That interpretation misses the essential point. Grant was not indifferent to casualties, nor was every decision he made successful. The assaults at Cold Harbor were a grave mistake. But his purpose was not to exchange lives indiscriminately. He understood that the Confederate army in Virginia was the principal military obstacle to Union victory, and he refused to allow Lee to escape the consequences of sustained pressure. Previous commanders had repeatedly withdrawn after bloody encounters, allowing Lee to recover, regroup, and regain the initiative. Grant did something different. After the Wilderness, he moved south. After Spotsylvania, he moved south again. After Cold Harbor, he did not retreat. And Lee never returned to the offensive.  

He recognized that the war would not be won by occupying a succession of places while leaving the principal Confederate army intact. Lee's army had to be kept under pressure until its capacity to resist was destroyed.

Lee himself understood the danger of Grant reaching the James River. He reportedly told Jubal Early that the Army of Northern Virginia must destroy Grant's army before it got there; otherwise, he believed, it would become merely a question of time. The remark was perceptive. Once Grant crossed the James, he would be positioned to threaten Richmond and Petersburg from the south, endanger the railroads supplying Lee's army, and establish a powerful logistical base from which to continue operations.

The crossing of the James in June 1864 was one of the most remarkable logistical achievements of the war. Grant moved an immense army across a broad river, with its animals, artillery, wagons, and supplies, while constructing a pontoon bridge of extraordinary length. The movement was executed with remarkable speed and secrecy. The army crossed without the catastrophic loss of men and matériel that such an undertaking might easily have entailed. The crossing demonstrated that Grant's generalship was not simply a matter of persistence under fire. It required detailed planning, engineering, transportation, supply, timing, and an understanding of the enemy's expectations.

The result was the siege of Petersburg. Lee was increasingly compelled to defend Richmond and the railway system that sustained his army. Grant, meanwhile, had established himself in a position from which he could extend his lines, threaten Confederate communications, and steadily constrict the enemy's ability to operate. What Lee had feared had come to pass.

But the eastern campaign was only one part of Grant's larger design. He was simultaneously directing the operations of four major Union armies: those of Meade, Butler, Sheridan, and Sherman. Horace Porter, one of Grant's closest aides, captured the achievement with a memorable image. He described them as a "dashing four-in-hand, with Grant holding the reins."

Porter's point was that the Union armies, though operating at considerable distances from one another, were no longer moving like unrelated commands. They were cooperating to keep Confederate forces constantly occupied on their respective fronts and to prevent the enemy from concentrating the bulk of its strength against any one Union army. The Confederacy possessed shorter interior lines and could move troops rapidly by rail. Grant's answer was coordinated, sustained pressure across the entire theater of war.

This was grand strategy in its fullest sense. Grant was converting numerical and material superiority into coordinated military power. Previous Union commanders had enjoyed substantial advantages in men and supplies, but those advantages had not automatically produced victory. Grant made them effective by ensuring that the armies worked toward a common objective.

And here Sheridan enters the picture, indispensable to the story.

His victories in the Shenandoah Valley in 1864 destroyed the Confederate ability to use that region as a dependable avenue for invasion and supply. Sheridan's operations also devastated resources upon which Lee had depended. His success at Cedar Creek, following an initially disastrous Union situation, became one of the decisive military and psychological episodes of the final year of the war. Sheridan was an aggressive and formidable commander, precisely the sort of subordinate Grant knew how to employ.

Sheridan later offered one of the most eloquent assessments of Grant's generalship. Writing of his chief during the later campaigns, he observed:

"The effect of his discomfitures was to make him all the more determined to discharge successfully the stupendous trust committed to his care, and to bring into play the manifold resources of his well-ordered mind. He guided every subordinate then, and in the last days of the rebellion, with a fund of common sense and a superiority of intellect which have left an impress so distinct as to exhibit his great personality."

Sheridan concluded with words that deserve to be remembered:

"When his military history is analyzed after the lapse of years, it will show even more clearly than now that during these, as well as his previous campaigns, he was the steadfast center about and on which everything else turned."

That phrase, "the steadfast center," is an extraordinarily evocative description of Grant. One might call him a centripetal force: the commander whose presence, judgment, and direction drew the separate energies of the Union armies toward a common purpose. Sherman, Sheridan, Meade, and Butler were not interchangeable instruments, nor did Grant attempt to make them so. He understood their different abilities and gave them responsibilities suited to their talents. But their independent efforts were no longer independent in the strategic sense. Grant held them together.

Lincoln deserves his place in this achievement. He had endured the frustrations of successive commanders who failed to translate military advantages into decisive results. He recognized Grant's qualities and, unlike his predecessors, was prepared to give him the authority and freedom necessary to prosecute the war. Lincoln told him: "You are vigilant and self-reliant; and, pleased with this, I wish not to obtrude any constraints or restraints upon you." That confidence was essential. Lincoln supplied the political leadership and sustained the national purpose; Grant supplied the overarching military direction.

The political dimension cannot be separated from the military one. The presidential election of 1864 was a genuine turning point. The Democratic platform called for an immediate cessation of hostilities and a convention to seek peace. McClellan (of all people), the Democratic nominee, was personally committed to restoring the Union, but his candidacy carried the possibility of an armistice and negotiations at a moment when the Confederacy still hoped to secure independence. A different electoral result might have altered the course of the war profoundly. The Union victories at Mobile Bay, in the Shenandoah Valley, and above all at Atlanta helped restore Northern confidence and contributed substantially to Lincoln's reelection. Grant's military strategy therefore had consequences far beyond the battlefield. It helped preserve the political conditions necessary for ultimate victory.

By the spring of 1865, the consequences of Grant's coordinated pressure were unmistakable. Sherman had completed his march through Georgia and was advancing through the Carolinas. Sheridan had helped close the avenues of Confederate escape and reinforcement in Virginia. Grant had extended his lines around Petersburg, steadily threatening the railroads and supply routes upon which Lee depended. The Confederate position was collapsing under pressure from several directions.

When Lee finally abandoned Petersburg and Richmond, Grant pursued. Sheridan's cavalry played a crucial role in preventing Lee from escaping westward. At Appomattox Court House, on April 9, 1865, Lee surrendered the Army of Northern Virginia. The date was exactly one year after Grant had issued his instructions to Meade declaring that the Union armies should move together toward one common center.

The coincidence is striking. The strategic conception expressed in that April 9 directive had become reality. The Union armies had been made to operate as parts of a coordinated whole, and the Confederacy could no longer sustain the war.

There is another interesting footnote to this remarkable group of commanders. Grant and Sherman were born in Ohio, at Point Pleasant and Lancaster respectively. Sheridan was born in New York but raised in Somerset, Ohio. All three were graduates of West Point, although their class standings were quite different. Sherman graduated sixth in a class of forty-two; Grant twenty-first in a class of thirty-nine; Sheridan thirty-fourth in a class of fifty-two. Their subsequent careers offer a useful reminder that academic standing is a poor measure of military greatness. The three men, formed in different circumstances and possessing markedly different temperaments, became the principal military figures in the Union's final campaigns.

Lincoln, Grant, and Sherman make a compelling triumvirate: political leadership, grand strategy, and operational execution. Sheridan must stand beside them as an essential member of the military achievement, especially in the decisive operations of the final year. The familiar stamp bearing the portraits of Sherman, Grant, and Sheridan, with Grant occupying the center, seems almost symbolic of the relationship.

Grant's greatness, however, should not be reduced to his association with two brilliant subordinates. His achievement was larger than that. He understood that the war could not be won by a collection of disconnected victories. It required the simultaneous application of military pressure, the destruction of Confederate armies as effective fighting forces, the disruption of the resources sustaining them, and the preservation of the Union's political will to continue.

He made the Union's armies pull together. He gave their separate movements coherence. He understood the relationship between geography, logistics, military operations, and political purpose. He could recognize the talents of others without feeling compelled to overshadow them, and he possessed the determination to continue when others might have recoiled from the cost.

There were brilliant battlefield commanders in the Civil War. There were bold strategists, gifted cavalrymen, and resourceful campaigners. Grant was something more unusual: a commander capable of holding the entire military effort in his mind and directing it toward a single end.

Sheridan's words remain the most fitting tribute. Grant was the steadfast center about and on which everything else turned.

That is the essence of his greatness as a grand strategist. He did not merely command armies. He made them an army.

text:
Ty Lue says he was making $375,000 as an assistant coach with the Clippers when the Cavaliers offered him $1,000,000 to become their associate head coach, and says he turned it down because he wanted to remain loyal to Doc Rivers, when they asked him what it would take he said $2,000,000 thinking there was no way they would pay that, but they immediately said yes and Jerry West told him he had to take it or might not get another big opportunity

“We interviewed at the same time for the job, right? My agent called me and was like, ‘Dan Gilbert decided that he wanted to go with David Blatt, but I got a crazy thing to tell you. They want you to be the associate head coach.’ And I was like, ‘No, I’m cool. I’m going to stay here with Doc.’”

“Because I figured if I’m with Doc, who’s the best coach in the league, I’m going to get a job next year. It’s coming, so I’m not going to leave Doc. I’m going to be loyal to Doc. And then my agent said, ‘But you wouldn’t believe how much money they offered you.’”

“I was like, ‘Well, what’d they offer?’ He said, ‘They want to offer you a million dollars a year to be the associate head coach.’ And at the time, I’m making $375,000 with the Clippers. I still said no. I was like, ‘No, I’m going to stay with Doc.’ My agent was like, ‘You sure?’ And I was like, ‘Yeah, I can’t do it.’ So they came back an hour later with another offer, and I was like, ‘No, man, I’m going to stay with Doc. I ain’t going to do that. I’m going to be loyal to Doc.’”

“So I called B-Shaw, and he said, ‘Man, you got to take that job.’ I said, ‘Man, I ain’t doing it.’ Then I called Jerry West, who’s my mentor, right? And Jerry was like, ‘What are you thinking? If you don’t take this job, they’ll never give you another job again. They’ll think you can’t leave Doc’s umbrella.’ So I was like, ‘Man, I’m not doing it.’ My agent called back again and said, ‘They said, well, what do you want?’ I said, ‘Man, just tell them $2 million.’ He called me back and said they said yes.”

“So I was like, ‘All right, I gotta go.’ I called Doc, and Doc was like, ‘You know what, Ty? It’s going to be hard for us to match that, but I think you’re ready to leave my umbrella, spread your wings, and do your own thing.’ He said, ‘I think it’d be good for you.’ And I was like, ‘You sure?’ He’s like, ‘Man, I think it’ll be really good for you.’ So that’s kind of how it happened. That’s how I ended up going to Cleveland.”

text:
A young teenage girl in Fairfax County, Virginia, was at the center of a sexual abuse case. The accused offender, illegal alien Ander Josue Cortez Mendez, was arrested. ICE asked Fairfax County to hold him.

The county refused.

Then came the goddamn plea bargain.

Mendez pleaded guilty to a reduced misdemeanor involving a child fifteen or older and received a three-month sentence, every fucking day suspended.

Three months. Zero days to serve.

What in the actual fuck is wrong with the people running this system?

Explain how a case involving allegations against a much younger victim ended with a reduced charge and a completely suspended sentence. Explain who signed off on that deal. Explain how the girl's interests were protected while the offender walked away without serving a day of that sentence.

And while you're explaining that disgrace, consider what prosecutors in New York actually put in writing.

The Bronx District Attorney's office produced an “Immigration-Conscious Plea Bargaining” guide recommending that prosecutors offer charges omitting a child's age as an element of a sexual offense to avoid certain immigration consequences.

Let that fucking obscenity sink in.

A child's age can determine whether a conviction triggers deportation consequences, and these taxpayer-funded legal contortionists actually developed written guidance explaining how to negotiate around that element.

How fucking twisted do your priorities have to become before you start treating the age of a sexually abused child as an inconvenient obstacle to keeping an offender in America?

The Fairfax prosecutor maintained the plea reflected the evidence. Fine. Then lay every goddamn decision on the table. Explain the reduced charge, the suspended sentence, and the declined ICE detainer.

And make every official defending these immigration-conscious prosecution policies explain precisely whose interests they're serving.

I'm sick of the sanctimonious bullshit about compassion from politicians whose criminal justice priorities deserve this kind of scrutiny.

Where was the compassion for that girl? Where was the outrage over what happened to her? Where was the fucking determination to hold the offender accountable?

A child deserved protection, justice, and a government willing to fight for her.

Instead, the public is left staring at a declined ICE detainer, a reduced conviction, and a sentence that required zero days behind bars.

So here's what every smug, self-righteous bastard responsible for these decisions should have to do:

Look that girl in the eyes. Explain every fucking choice.

And answer the question that should haunt every official involved:

When the government was deciding how much this man would suffer for his crime, who the fuck was fighting for the child who suffered because of it?

New Shorts from the writer who wears shorts

Written for those with short attention spans

EAST CLINTWOOD

The world’s worst detective is accidentally the only one who can solve the case.

Bradley Pritchett, mild-mannered Ohio insurance adjuster, wakes from a three-week coma and discovers his brain has been replaced by a 1940s radio drama.

He is now East Clintwood: fedora, rumpled trench coat over a hospital gown, smoky voice-over narration, and zero actual detective skills. He doesn’t remember his wife, his kids, or his old life. He only remembers “the case of the century”—The Vanishing Violinist—a conspiracy his injured mind invented from a tune he was humming right before the crash.

Armed with a notebook of “clues” that are actually grocery lists, parking tickets, and his daughter’s crayon drawings, East enthusiastically bungles his way through suburbia. He waves at the people he’s supposed to be tailing. He falls asleep on stakeouts. He offers suspects coffee and asks if they’ve seen anything “fishy.” His teenage daughter becomes “my plucky secretary, Penny.” His wife is “the dame who still owes me expenses.”

Then the joke stops being a joke.

While chasing a mailman who “always delivers at 10:07 sharp,” East stumbles onto a real insurance-fraud ring operating inside the company Bradley used to work for. The criminals assume the guy in the thrift-store fedora is harmless.

They’re wrong—not because East is brilliant, but because he is stubbornly, unshakably committed to the wrong case.

Every ridiculous misinterpretation somehow points him at the right people.
The comedy stays warm. The family slowly realizes this version of Bradley is more alive than the original ever was. And the climax turns on one last absurd clue that, against all odds, happens to be true.

Does Bradley ever come back? Or does East Clintwood keep the fedora and open the worst detective agency in Ohio?

Think The Pink Panther meets Memento meets Fletch, with a heart. A fish-out-of-water comedy that accidentally becomes a crime story, carried by a lovable disaster who narrates his own life like it’s already a classic

Coffee with The Reaper

Tired of life? Maybe death is the upgrade.
Meet Frank Delgado—loyal husband, overworked dad, and all-around nice guy who just checked out… permanently.

Heart Attack

Now he’s stuck in a late-night diner across from the Grim Reaper, who’s pouring coffee and pitching the deal of a lifetime:
“Sell me your soul and I’ll give you more years on Earth!”

Sounds tempting… until Frank remembers what’s waiting for him back home:
a lazy, money stealing wife, a 23-year-old stripper son who empties the fridge, and a 26-year-old “college student” still on year eight with zero degrees all on Frank’s dime.

For once, Frank says the one word Death never expects:
“No.”

A hilarious, heartwarming tale of one man who finally finds peace… by staying dead.

Sometimes the best second chance… is no second chance at all.

Jolene Must Die

Did You Think You Could Actually Take My Man?

A dark twist flipping Dolly Parton’s “Jolene” into psychological terror

In the quiet corners of her mind, Alizabeth saw it all unfold the moment Jolene’s eyes lingered a second too long on her man. One glance was all it took. From that instant, a beautiful stranger became a calculated thief, and an ordinary day became the start of a secret affair that existed nowhere but inside Alizabeth’s head. 

Freddy never met Jolene. He never even learned her name. But Alizabeth watched, followed, and collected every innocent moment as damning proof, spinning a private war against a rival who had no idea she was in a rivalry.

What begins as jealous suspicion hardens into obsession, then into something far darker. With every misread smile and imagined betrayal, Alizabeth’s devotion twists into a chilling vow: Jolene will never take her man… because Alizabeth will make sure she never gets the chance

📢 𝗝𝗨𝗦𝗧 𝗜𝗡: WALL STREET’S $𝟱𝟬𝟬 𝗕𝗜𝗟𝗟𝗜𝗢𝗡 $NVDA NVIDIA CHIP FINANCING PLAN HAS YET TO FUND A DEAL - $AMD $AVGO 

Six Wall Street firms set out in August to help Nvidia customers finance chip purchases. The partnership has yet to deploy any capital, The Wall Street Journal reports.

The sticking point is who bears the risk. Nvidia offered to back up to 𝟮𝟱% of a project’s cost, and investors want more protection before lending to lower-rated borrowers.

👉 𝗞𝗲𝘆 𝗛𝗶𝗴𝗵𝗹𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁𝘀

➤ 𝗣𝗟𝗘𝗗𝗚𝗘 𝗧𝗘𝗥𝗠𝗦: Apollo, Blackstone, BlackRock, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR signed a memorandum setting a $500 billion fundraising target. It leaves each firm free to decide whether to raise money and Nvidia to review guarantees case by case.

➤ 𝗖𝗛𝗜𝗣 𝗗𝗘𝗠𝗔𝗡𝗗: The goal was to make chip financing a standard investment for lenders so customers ranging from OpenAI and Anthropic to smaller startups could keep buying Nvidia chips.

➤ 𝗕𝗥𝗢𝗔𝗗𝗖𝗢𝗠 𝗖𝗢𝗠𝗣𝗔𝗥𝗜𝗦𝗢𝗡: Broadcom guaranteed the residual value of about 𝟴𝟱% of a $35 billion Anthropic financing deal. Its guarantee covered just under three-quarters of a $63 billion follow-up deal.

➤ 𝗢𝗣𝗘𝗡𝗔𝗜 𝗕𝗔𝗖𝗞𝗦𝗧𝗢𝗣: Nvidia shares fell 5% after WSJ reported it was considering a $250 billion guarantee for an OpenAI data center in Ohio. Nvidia subsequently cut its initial commitment in half.

➤ 𝗙𝗜𝗥𝗦𝗧 𝗗𝗘𝗔𝗟: Talks continue on the partnership’s first chip-backed financing for an Nvidia customer. People familiar with the discussions told WSJ they expect it to close 𝗻𝗼 𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗹𝗶𝗲𝗿 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝗻 𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟳.

👉 𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗲𝗿𝘁 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀:

𝗖𝗼𝗹𝗲𝘁𝘁𝗲 𝗞𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘀, Nvidia interim CEO, on the earnings call: “We are rigorously evaluating future investments, commitments and guarantees.”

𝗠𝗮𝗿𝗰 𝗥𝗼𝘄𝗮𝗻, Apollo CEO, warned that many AI cloud providers could lose access to financing if Nvidia steps back as a guarantor.

Source: The Wall Street Journal | $NVDA $AVGO

text:
Online, people are blaming the FAA's AI system, SMART, for the ground stop. The FAA's Q&A says: "No. The two systems are not related. SMART is a data aggregator, and it does not feed information into the air traffic control system." Duffy says SMART "had zero impact." The vendor, Air Space Intelligence, says the same. So does MIT's R. John Hansman, via PolitiFact, who says it has no direct connection to the comm system.

Now the contract, read directly on https://t.co/feByU70yJP. Award 693KA726C00064, FAA to Air Space Intelligence, signed June 23, 2026, running to 2038. The ceiling is $875,950,000. That is potential value, not money paid. Obligated so far: $23,340,500. Twelve offers. The record describes "flow management data and services." The word SMART is not in the part we read, and PolitiFact says the contract covers SMART and another system.

The donation: Air Space Intelligence's PAC gave $2,500 in March to Rep.-elect Michael Alfonso, Republican of Wisconsin and Duffy's son-in-law, per PolitiFact and the Washington Examiner. We have not opened the FEC record. We found no evidence that SMART caused the stop, or that the donation influenced the award. Neither Duffy nor the FAA has said whether Duffy was personally involved in the award. So was he?
OFFICIAL, the contract figures (USAspending record, read directly; one source)
CLAIM, "not related" (FAA and the vendor are interested parties, plus one expert)
CLAIM, the donation figure (two outlets, FEC record not opened)
VERDICT (our opinion): the AI-caused-the-shutdown claim fails; the donation is a fair procurement question with no evidence of influence found.

text:
My son recently started mowing lawns around our neighborhood in suburban New Jersey to save money for his first car.

He charges $35 per lawn and usually works on Saturday mornings.

Last weekend, he noticed that an elderly neighbor's front yard was badly overgrown.

The man had been struggling to maintain it, so my son offered to mow it for free.

The neighbor thanked him, and my son spent nearly an hour cleaning everything up.

Two days later, another neighbor came knocking at our door.

She claimed my son had violated neighborhood rules by operating an unauthorized landscaping business and demanded that we stop him from using residential properties for commercial activities.

I explained that he hadn't charged the elderly man anything.

She said that wasn't the point and threatened to contact the homeowners association.

Now she's also complaining that other teenagers might start knocking on doors offering services.

My son was trying to help an elderly neighbor, and somehow he's become the neighborhood problem.

text:
Tonight’s energy at the YMCA back room is pure kinetic potential, a rebound in motion, waiting for the next collision. 

Jensen Huang’s exit from Nvidia has the market oscillating between relief and rupture with third quarter revenue more than doubled to one hundred fifteen point eight billion dollars, guidance lifted to seventy-five percent growth for fiscal twenty-eight.

Chairman Harvey Jones has unanimously ruled out reinstating him, even as he publicly offered to return. Elon Musk, at the New York Times DealBook Summit, called it kicking Michael Jordan off the Bulls mid winning streak, Jensen as peak Jordan, irreplaceable in supply chain diplomacy and decades deep supplier relationships across Korea and Taiwan. 

That tension, performance versus principle, is the fault line. The tape may drift sideways or catch a short term optimism boost from Trump’s presence in Shenzhen at APEC, where he’s floated eventually permitting Blackwell sales to China once they’re no longer frontier while the administration just issued a ninety-day rule tightening remote compute access for Chinese AI labs through Southeast Asian data centers. 

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick travels with him, already under bipartisan fire for delayed action on Megaspeed. But the real catalyst isn’t earnings. It’s testimony. Jensen has agreed to appear before the Senate Banking Committee under Tim Scott, with Lutnick following; House panels want him December first. That Capitol Hill collision is where national security and shareholder value stop being abstract.

Colette Kress deserves the congratulations. She delivered the quarter, raised guidance, pledged capital discipline, and quietly redirected Nvidia’s virtue from pure compute expansion toward energy, land, power, and shell backstops, including a four-point-five-gigawatt Portsmouth commitment. 

That’s the deeper signal. In any complex system, the binding constraint migrates from the processor to the power plant. Compute is now abundant; electrons and protons are not. The next phase won’t be about who builds the fastest chip. It’ll be about who secures the watt.

I welcome every perspective, because in a system this entangled, truth isn’t in any single node. It’s in the interference pattern between them.

One thing worth watching! Anthropic’s IPO drops tomorrow, and it’ll be the cleanest read on whether AI investor appetite survived the Nvidia shock. @POTUS @elonmusk @JensenHuang @nvidia @BillAckman

text:
A company is not its buildings, its patents or its stock price.

A company is a group of people who decided to follow someone.

This week we got to watch what happens when a board forgets that.

Nvidia posted the best quarter in its history.
Then the people who built that quarter started signing their names.
A reported 10,000 employees, a quarter of the company, put it in a letter.
A petition passed 200,000 signatures.
Elon Musk said removing Jensen is like the Bulls kicking Michael Jordan off the team in the middle of a winning streak.
The President said he “can’t be replaced.”
The founder of Uber offered to show up with a megaphone.

And the board? Reportedly calling other CEOs.
History has run this experiment before.
In 1985, Apple’s board chose the professional manager over the founder.
It took them eleven years, and a company near bankruptcy, to admit the mistake.
In 1998, the Bulls won 62 games. Jordan left.
The next season they won 13. Same arena. Same logo.
The lesson is always the same, and it is always learned late.

Loyalty is not a line item.
You cannot buy it, you cannot transfer it, and you cannot vote it onto a new CEO.

A board can remove a founder with a show of hands.
It cannot remove the reason people stayed.

When the workers, the owners and the rivals all agree,
and a handful of people in a boardroom disagree,
the boardroom is not the adult in the room.
It is the problem in the room.
Boards can fire a founder in a day.
Replacing one takes a decade.

$SPY $QQQ MARKET UPDATE: CASH IS A POSITION TOO.

After hitting every bearish target yesterday, including the $735 gap fill and the 200-day SMA retest near $727–730, I closed my remaining puts and moved entirely into cash.

I stayed in cash today, and here’s why:

I don’t see a particularly strong directional edge.

Bulls are looking at a potential double bottom and arguing the lows are in. Bears see a possible head and shoulders structure and bear flag, suggesting another leg lower.

Both interpretations are plausible. Neither is confirmed.

1. SPY The levels that matter

SPY remains in a bearish structure, with declining moving averages overhead.

The first major resistance is $741–742, followed by the more important $750–751 zone.

A rally that fails at either level could simply be a dead cat bounce before another sell off.

For me, reclaiming $741 is only the first step. A sustained move above $751, followed by improving daily moving average structure, would make the bullish reversal argument considerably stronger.

Until then, I’m treating any bounce as a potential relief rally within a downtrend.

2. QQQ Similar structure, different levels

QQQ is showing comparable weakness.

The first meaningful resistance sits around $679–680, where the 100 EMA on the 4 hour chart is also located.

Above that, $695–700 is the more important zone to reclaim.

A recovery that repeatedly fails beneath those levels would favour the bearish continuation scenario.

Conversely, sustained acceptance above them would suggest buyers are regaining control.

3. What if the market makes another low?

This is actually the scenario I’d prefer for potential long entries.

On SPY, I’m watching $720–721, around the 50-week SMA, followed by the $715–716 liquidity/support area.

That $715–721 region could offer a much cleaner risk/reward opportunity for calls, provided buyers defend it.

If it fails, $711 becomes another downside level to monitor.

For QQQ, I’m watching $635, followed by $621–622 if that support breaks.

These are potential reaction zones, not automatic buy signals. A level is only useful if price confirms it.

4. VIX, oil and tomorrow’s Anthropic IPO

VIX hasn’t given me convincing evidence that volatility is ready to collapse.

A pullback towards 22-20 could still find support and produce another volatility expansion, pressuring equities again.

Oil has also been selling off sharply alongside the market. If oil finds support and reverses, I’ll be watching how equities react.

We also have Anthropic’s IPO tomorrow. It’ll be interesting to see whether the listing draws liquidity away from other technology stocks or instead boosts sentiment across the AI sector.

For now, none of these factors provides a decisive directional signal.

5. My preferred scenario

If SPY and QQQ rally on Thursday or Friday but fail at the resistance zones above, I’d still lean towards a dead cat bounce followed by another potential sell off next week.

If buyers reclaim the levels I mentioned and the technical structure improves I’ll start leaning towards a full recovery.

If we instead sell off towards my preferred lower support zones, I’ll start looking to position in longs.

BOTTOM LINE

I was bearish when the technical evidence favoured the downside. That trade is finished, and the profits are secured.

Now the market needs to show its hand.

Calling a bottom because you want one isn’t analysis. Neither is remaining bearish simply because your previous short thesis worked.

Trading is about identifying an edge, defining invalidation and adapting to price action.

Right now, I see competing scenarios rather than a compelling entry.

And when there’s no clear edge, I have absolutely no problem sitting in cash.

Patience is part of the strategy. You don’t have to trade every move.

Prosecutor ASA Alixandra Buckelew and the State of Florida filed 5 Motion To Strike against YNW Melly, real name Jamell Demons, with the Broward County Clerk on Wednesday, November 18. 

In the 5-page motion, the prosecution’s Motion To Strike YNW Melly’s Motion In Limine To Exclude Rap Lyrics And/Or Videos Filed on November 10 argues that the Defense’s Motion To Exclude violates the court's April 30, 2025, filing deadline, lacks good cause and threatens to delay a retrial that has already faced multiple postponements.

ASA Alixandra Buckelew claims YNW Melly’s defense filed the Motion to Exclude just 35 working days before trial and 7 working days before a scheduled motion hearing. The State argues that the defense offered no justification for the delay.

ASA Alixandra Buckelew and the State argue that they disclosed the rap lyrics in January 2024, and some lyrics and videos appeared during Demons' original trial. Therefore, YNW Melly’s defense had ample opportunity to challenge the evidence before the deadline.

If the Judge Martin S. Fein and the court considers the motion, the prosecution request additional preparation time and say they may need additional witnesses and experts if the evidence is challenged.

Judge Martin S. Fein has not ruled on these motions yet with a hearing set for November 23 and 24.

The motions follow YNW Melly’s attorneys, Drew Findling (@drewfindling) and Carey Haughwout, filing Motions to Exclude with the Broward County Clerk on November 13.

Hawley: "I want to introduce each of our witnesses and as I do so, give you the chance to make an opening statement. We'll start with Mr. Michael Schlep. Mr. Schlep is a survivor of childhood grooming and abuse on Roblox. He is now a content creator and a child safety advocate who has dedicated his platform to exposing online predators and raising awareness of child exploitation on Roblox. And I'll just say, Mr. Schlep, I had the opportunity to meet your parents who I think are sitting behind you and are very proud of the man that they raised and rightly so. We're delighted."

Schlep: "Chairman Hawley, ranking member Durban, and distinguished members of the subcommittee, thank you for inviting me to testify today. At age eight, I, like millions of other American children, created my first Roblox account. My parents thought it was a kid-friendly educational game. They didn't realize that I would be accessible to strangers across the world.

When I was 12, a user invited me to an official Roblox chat room where I met a famous game developer by the name of Kevin Nolan. He began helping me um with my own games as a kid. I didn't realize that Kevin was much older than me. He moved our chats to private spaces, positioning himself as someone I could trust, encouraging me to share my most vulnerable thoughts to him. He asked me to meet in person. I refused.

Over time, Kevin's fame grew and Roblox produced an official toy of his avatar. While I was exposed to increasingly disturbing content in our online communications, including BDSM and violent pornography, cartel beheadings, and extreme racist ideologies like the Christurch mass shooting video in 2019. Meanwhile, his toy was sold in stores and featured in commercials all across the country. This is a toy here. When I finally built up the courage to leave Kevin, he publicly leaked my private confessions he had manipulated out of me. The torment culminated in a suicide attempt and a psychiatric hospitalization.

I later returned to Roblox, hoping to build a safer community through my YouTube channel. Soon, young viewers began messaging me about their own Roblox predators. I realized what happened to me wasn't an isolated incident, but a much larger systemic problem. Then I watched Roblox file a $1.6 million lawsuit to silence a whistleblower by the name of Benjamin Simon. That was my breaking point. Instead of catching predators, Roblox was more concerned with stopping people from pointing out how many predators are on their platform.

To expose the problem, I launched a YouTube channel, Schlep. What I uncovered was unimaginable. Predators, sexing groups, violent and graphic pornography, even child sexual abuse material rings operating and profiting on Roblox through its virtual currency, Robux.

Partnering with a predator catching group with over 400 convictions across 49 states, I caught six predators within 10 months, resulting in four convictions. One admitted to me personally that he had groomed hundreds of minors on the platform. I received emails saying, "You got my groomer arrested" from children. Where Roblox failed them, I succeeded.

Until my videos. Roblox failed to ban these accounts. I begged them for a private reporting line. I mailed physical binders to their headquarters and even offered to sign a contract to help them for free. Instead, I received a cease and desist letter from Roblox, terminating my accounts and threatening to sue me. When it back when it backlashed, sparking the #FreeSchlep movement, they banned users and games protesting.

The Louisiana Attorney General and several states sued Roblox, citing games I exposed, such as Dollhouse Roleplay, a game used by 764, a group the FBI has designated as a terrorist organization. Roblox claims it has changed, but their new age verification system is very easy for child predators to bypass. Kidnappings and murders related to Roblox are still happening.

Despite all these new features, Roblox funnels their users onto a platform known as Discord, one of the National Center for Online Sexual Exploitation's Dirty Dozens list for as a dangerous platform.

Roblox claims there's no textbased image sharing on the platform, but it allows you to upload images onto it, which I've seen child sexual abuse material, suicides, and cartel mutilations being uploaded onto the so-called children's platform despite parental controls being enabled. According to their employees, Roblox puts, and I quote, "making investors happy above their child safety". CEO David Baszucki dismissed child predator crisis on the platform as an "opportunity to improve safety". Worst of all, law enforcement is not allowed to conduct investigations on their platform. While Roblox banned me, the police have welcomed my help. Just last month, I demonstrated how and where to find predators on Roblox to the Pulk County Sheriff's Office in Florida.

Roblox must be held accountable publicly. They will not voluntarily act to protect children. Law enforcement, Congress, and state legislators must act. Hundreds of families have filed civil cases. But unsurprisingly, Roblox is trying to force those children who have been whose abuse it facilitated out of court into a secret and rigged forced arbitration system. They must be stopped. and these families must be encountered or empowered to seek accountability in court.

Thank you and I am stand ready to support this committee in stopping online platforms for enabling and profiting off of the abuse of children."

Hawley: "Thank you very much Mr. Schlep."

This happened yesterday and I am still a bit riled up by it. 

My wife and I recently moved to California for work. We left all our friends and family behind. My wife had trouble adapting as she was feeling a bit lonely. I had co-workers I was able to build friendships with, but my wife did not. 

A few weeks ago my wife was very excited to tell me she made a new friend while out that day. Over the weeks, my wife and her new friend frequently texted, went out for dinner/drinks a few times, and talked on the phone. I was happy my wife was adapting to our new life and made a best friend. Her new friend was about the same age as us, single but on bumble, and she shared other details about their common interests but nothing really relevant to the story.

text:
$500B NVIDIA CHIP-FINANCING PLAN HAS DEPLOYED ZERO CAPITAL, WITH NO DEALS EXPECTED BEFORE 2027: WSJ

In June, Wall Street giants Apollo Global Management and Blackstone announced a megadeal to help Broadcom, one of Nvidia’s main rivals, secure $35 billion of chip financing for Anthropic.

Huang, then CEO of NVIDIA, was irate, people close to the situation said. He’d been talking about a similar program and felt the progress was too slow, so he summoned several titans of Wall Street to California, the people said. Huang wanted a bigger deal and fast.

In August, NVIDIA announced a partnership with Apollo, Blackstone, BlackRock, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR to mobilize $500B to help customers like OpenAI, Anthropic and smaller AI cloud companies finance chip purchases.

But the agreement was only a few-page memorandum of understanding. None of the firms was obligated to raise any money, and no capital has been deployed.

Jensen Huang had initially pushed for an even larger $1T financing program, partly to support Nvidia's valuation as its earnings grew but its valuation multiple declined.

He accelerated the effort after Apollo and Blackstone helped rival Broadcom arrange $35B in chip financing for Anthropic.

The biggest obstacle has been Nvidia's willingness to guarantee the loans:

Nvidia was willing to provide credit support covering up to 25% of project costs.

Broadcom provided residual-value guarantees covering about 85% of Anthropic's $35B Project Big Sky and just under 75% of its $63B Project North Star.

As lenders have become more cautious about AI financing, they have pushed Nvidia to offer greater protection.

Nvidia has also been pulling back its financial guarantees. Earlier, reports of a proposed $250B Nvidia backstop for an OpenAI data center sent NVIDIA shares down 5%, prompting Nvidia to cut its initial commitment in half.

Interim CEO Colette Kress has since signaled that future investments and guarantees will be evaluated more strictly.

Talks on the partnership's first chip-backed financing deal are still underway, but nothing is expected to close before 2027.

Apollo CEO Marc Rowan warned that without Nvidia providing financial guarantees, a large number of neocloud companies could lose access to capital.

Nvidia had already begun to rein in the backstops and guarantees it uses to grease lending, partly under the skepticism of finance chief Colette Kress, who has now become the interim CEO. 

Those guarantees are crucial to Wall Street’s willingness to finance the chips, and Kress on Tuesday signaled to investors that the company will be disciplined in the deals it supports.

Meanwhile, NVIDIA this Quarter reporte that Purchase commitments $390BN went up from $279BN, while Leases and cloud deals were just above $100BN. Neocloud agreements commitments stood at $32BN & Guarantees at $118BN

Total tally of everything off the balance sheet for NVIDIA has gone up t $668BN, up from $530.5BN in just one quarter.

California Rep. Mike Levin is sounding the alarm over President Trump’s nomination of Eric Ueland to lead the Government Accountability Office, claiming Americans can kiss accountability goodbye if he’s confirmed.

That’s quite a verdict before the Senate has even questioned the nominee.

Ueland serves as the No. 2 official at the Office of Management and Budget under Russell Vought. His nomination raises legitimate questions about independence, particularly given disputes over presidential spending authority.

But Levin offers no evidence that Ueland intends to conceal fraud, manipulate audits or abandon the GAO’s statutory responsibilities.

The comptroller general serves a 15-year term precisely to provide continuity and independence across administrations.

Levin also questions why the bipartisan congressional recommendation commission reportedly never met. That procedural concern deserves an explanation.

Congress should thoroughly scrutinize Ueland’s qualifications, independence and approach to executive spending authority.

But declaring a nominee corrupt or incapable of oversight simply because he worked for Trump isn’t accountability. It’s partisan prejudgment.

Let the hearing happen. Ask difficult questions. Demand substantive answers.

That’s how oversight is supposed to work.

The problem I would say is one of belief. 
Members believe in the gospel, in the faith, and in the ordinances and actions taken in churches and temples. We believe it sincerely and with full weight. 
I imagine you do not. Which makes all the money spent and the long scope of the human story being prepared for by members through expansion of those things as being wasteful and unnecessary. 

I get that tbh. Ask me ten years ago and I would have been right there with you saying something similar. 

Faith changes that. Either you have genuine faith that sees that, or you don't and it becomes more important to value the moment and uplifting everyone in this moment out of their filth because if the church were to give away all the money, everyone would have a billion dollars each. (exaggeration of course). 

But, believers want disciples willing to change themselves and the world not just to have their predicament changed. I found faith and I demanded God grant me the change I sought at first. It did nothing to help my situation. It wasn't until I began to change and seek the Lord's help in changing that I saw real true lasting hope for a better life begin and be built. 

But I get it, giving that kind of faith is hard and it's easier to demand those with give to those without with no requirements.

And, I would argue you're right. We, as disciples, are asked to consecrate our lives that way. And that's what I am doing. But, that's not the same as saying the tithing money or the church services should be exhausted fully or that members should stop tithing because there's a bunch. Both are tracks we are meant to run on in my mind. 

To offer our Christ-like support without attachment to something and to give unto the Lord His tithing to help support the growth and strengthening of the faith in the world in preparation for the future we do not yet know or understand. 

So make it a trillion is important to me as it testifies of our willingness to believe and have faith in the doctrine we claim to support by seeking exponential expansion of temple and churches. Cover the world with them.

But also, serve and support our fellow humans of all kinds with love and support in order to help them build out of their circumstance to a better life and knowing God our Father and Jesus Christ. 

We can do both. We should do both. If we believe. 

If we don't believe, well, then I hope people do things like you and others do and at least push people to Do Better and be better humans somehow. Even if I disagree with it and it may only serve the current moment. It's still better than the alternative...drowning in despair, in nihilistic service to the self, and hopeless sustained living without purpose of any kind.

Jesus’ Words on the Widow’s Offering
In Mark 12:41–44, Jesus sat opposite the temple treasury and watched the crowd putting money in. Many rich people gave large amounts, but a poor widow came and placed two small copper coins — worth only a few cents. Jesus called His disciples to Him and said, “Truly I tell you, this poor widow has put more into the treasury than all the others. They all gave out of their wealth; but she, out of her poverty, put in everything — all she had to live on”
Meaning and Application
Jesus’ words emphasize that the value of a gift is not measured by the amount given, but by the proportion of one’s resources that is offered. The widow’s offering, though small in monetary terms, represented her entire livelihood, showing complete trust and sacrifice. This contrasts with the rich who gave from surplus, often leaving their needs met.
Chairty, the Willingness to Give to Help Others less fortunate; Why is it important to know this truth?
Because in the life of charity, all growth comes from God, but at the same time he does not will to save us without us (1 Cor 3:6, CCC 1847). In an election-night post and a PBS NewsHour interview, Oklahoma City’s Republican mayor, David Holt, delivered a stark warning about what Trumpism has done to his party. 
Holt’s post-election diagnosis reaches back a decade. In his view, Republicans did more than nominate Donald Trump: they gradually surrendered the party’s judgment and identity to him. Holt said the GOP “ceded our decision-making and our intellectual capacity to one person,” trading a party of ideas and coalition-building for a vehicle for Trumpism. After the midterm losses, he called the result a rejection of MAGA and said the movement no longer functioned as a conventional political force. 

The warning was there in 2016. Lindsey Graham said, “If we nominate Trump, we will get destroyed … and we will deserve it.” He warned that Trump would destroy the party he loved. But after Trump took control of the party, Graham’s opposition gave way to alliance. He became one of Trump’s most dependable Senate supporters. 

Graham was not alone. Ted Cruz called Trump a “pathological liar” and “utterly amoral,” then endorsed him after first telling convention delegates to “vote your conscience.” Marco Rubio called Trump a serious threat to the party and the country, warned he would fracture the GOP, and later offered to help him. Cruz and Rubio too, went on to become a prominent Trump allies.

That is the part of Holt’s argument that cuts deepest: the party’s transformation was not imposed from outside. Republican leaders saw the danger, said so publicly, and then recalculated when Trump’s hold on the party became clear. Some may have believed they could work with him, steer him or preserve their own influence. Instead, the party increasingly followed his lead.

Holt is not saying the country no longer needs conservative politics. He says it needs a competent center-right party with ideas and a platform. His warning is that Republicans let a narrower, personality-driven movement take its place—and voters have now delivered the rebuke Graham predicted. Oklahoma remained Republican, Holt acknowledged, but he urged his party not to confuse a red-state stronghold with a national mandate.

text:
Appreciate the reply, Sherm! Big fan and looking forward to y’all’s coverage tomorrow.

Today’s cap is $301M, and it’s gone up an average of roughly 10% annually over the last 3 years.

For some perspective, Trevor Lawrence signed his extension after 3 seasons at 21.5% of the cap. I think that’s a pretty reasonable apples-to-apples comparison for Stroud after 3 years (although the ship on that has sailed and it will now be after 4 years). At today’s cap, that would be roughly $64.7M/year.

And that’s not some outrageous percentage for a franchise QB. Burrow got 24.5%, Herbert 23.4%, Hurts 22.7%, and Lawrence 21.5%. All signed after 3 seasons.

Stroud was reportedly offered somewhere in the mid-$50Ms and countered with a number that wouldn’t have made him the highest-paid QB and reportedly wanted to be team friendly to help with the cap.  (Mahomes currently highest at $64M APY). 

Now he’s playing better, and the cap isn’t going to stop increasing.

Even if we lower his valuation to just 20% of the cap, here’s what that looks like next year:

5% cap increase: $316.3M = $63.3M/year

10% cap increase: $331.3M = $66.3M/year

At Lawrence’s 21.5%, you’re looking at $68M–$71M annually.

To be clear, I’m using percentage of the cap in the year the deal is signed, not when the actual cap hits kick in. Just a consistent way to compare contracts across different years.

My point is that I already thought 21.5% was a reasonable valuation for Stroud, and with the way he’s playing right now, I think you could argue he’s worth even more.

He’s been one of the few bright spots on a struggling team, playing behind suspect pass protection, with one of the worst rushing attacks in football throughout his career, and now a defense that’s regressing too so far this season. 

I understand wanting to see more before committing that kind of money, but if you believe he’s your franchise QB, waiting can get expensive in a hurry. Especially if he keeps playing like one of the better QBs in the league.

Obviously factors like guaranteed money and length of the deal can lower the APY as well.

@rogla @NSNCyclingTeam @weare_NSN @andresiniesta8 @kjellcarlstrom @RichardCarapazM @SantiagoBS26 @GrmayeBiniam @georgenbennett #Vuelta2027 @wedusport 
Primož Roglič has signed a one-year contract with NSN Cycling Team for the 2027 season, announced on 18 November 2026. The 37-year-old Slovenian leaves Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe after three seasons and joins a Swiss WorldTour squad building general classification ambitions around a group of experienced leaders.

NSN framed the move as the “final chapter” of his career (“gremo!”), though neither side has confirmed retirement after 2027. Roglič remains motivated, citing the team’s “Never Say Never” name as a perfect fit.

The Signing and Immediate Context:
NSN Cycling Team (UCI WorldTeam, Swiss license, operations based in Girona with Catalan ties) announced the deal on its website. It is a one-year agreement covering only 2027—shorter than the multi-year deals given to other incoming GC riders. This followed months of speculation after his Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe contract expired.Options had included a rejected Lotto-Intermarché offer, a ruled-out return to Visma-Lease a Bike, interest from Tudor, Pinarello-Q36.5, Movistar and others, and even Unibet Rose Rockets (which withdrew for financial reasons).
Retirement was openly discussed; Red Bull boss Ralph Denk reportedly advised him to consider stepping away rather than joining a more modest project.

Roglič’s own words indicate he still has “some work to do—in both racing and with myself.”
He will join Richard Carapaz (signed through 2029), Santiago Buitrago and Lennert Van Eetvelt (also on longer deals). The group gives NSN its strongest GC roster yet.

Primož Roglič Career:
Born 29 October 1989, Roglič transitioned from ski jumping to professional cycling around 2012–13. He rode for Adria Mobil, then spent eight highly successful years at Jumbo-Visma (later Visma-Lease a Bike) before three seasons at Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe.

Key palmarès (93 career victories total):
4× Vuelta a España (2019, 2020, 2021, 2024)
Giro d’Italia (2023)
Olympic gold in the individual time trial (Tokyo 2021)
World Championships time-trial silver (2017)
Liège-Bastogne-Liège (2020)
Multiple stage-race wins and Grand Tour stage victories (especially in the Vuelta).

He is known for resilience, time-trial strength, climbing ability in Grand Tours, and a winning mentality that has produced consistent high-level results across more than a decade in the WorldTour.
2026 Season PerformanceRoglič’s 2026 campaign included setbacks and strong finishes. A training incident in late July (hit by a car) forced him to miss San Sebastián and the Vuelta a Burgos.

He still delivered

2nd overall at the Vuelta a España, 2 minutes 15 seconds behind winner Enric Mas (Movistar).
A fifth Vuelta title would have given him the outright record; he described the result positively given the circumstances of preparing for the race.
European Time Trial Champion on home soil in Šenčur, Slovenia (7 October 2026), winning the 22 km course in 28:16.61 ahead of Bruno Armirail.
Slovenian time-trial champion and solid results including 5th at Tirreno-Adriatico.

These late-season performances demonstrated he remains competitive at the highest level at age 37.

Primož Roglič will enter NSN as one of its primary general classification options in 2027, but not as an undisputed sole leader.

The team has assembled a crowded group of riders with Grand Tour ambitions, and Roglič’s experience and one-year “final chapter” framing position him as a high-priority option for at least one of the three Grand Tours—most logically the Vuelta a España, the race he has dominated more than any other.

Roglič brings the most proven three-week management experience on the roster: four Vuelta titles, a Giro win, Olympic time-trial gold, and a long track record of defending or chasing GC across all three Grand Tours.
At 37, his strengths remain time-trialing, resilience, and the ability to perform when it matters in the final week.

He joins three other riders who have also been given leadership language:

Richard Carapaz (signed through 2029): 2019 Giro winner, Olympic road-race gold, two Tour stage wins and the mountains classification in 2026, plus 8th overall at the Tour and 4th at the Vuelta that year.

Santiago Buitrago (longer deal): Giro stage winner, 2026 Vuelta mountains classification winner, and consistent top-10 Grand Tour finishes.

Lennert Van Eetvelt (longer deal): Winner of the 2024 UAE Tour and Tour of Guangxi; younger climber with stage-race GC potential.

With only three Grand Tours, the team will almost certainly split leadership. Roglič’s short contract and specialized Vuelta pedigree make him the natural lead when the calendar aligns with his strengths, while the others can co-lead, attack, or support depending on the race.
The group gives NSN tactical flexibility (multiple threats) but also the classic risk of diluted resources if all four are targeting the same objectives.

Support Riders for GC Ambitions:
True dedicated super-domestiques are limited compared with UAE, Visma, or Red Bull. The most relevant options include:

George Bennett (New Zealand, staying through 2027): Experienced climber and Grand Tour veteran (previous stints at Visma and UAE). Team management has highlighted his road-captaincy value as NSN increases its GC focus. He is the clearest pure support option among the veterans.

Kasper Asgreen: Time-trial and classics specialist who can protect on flatter stages and contribute in individual time trials.

Nick Schultz and other climbers already on the roster: Useful mountain support.
The co-leaders themselves (especially Buitrago and Van Eetvelt on days they are not racing for personal GC) can function as high-level helpers.

Younger or versatile riders (Artem Shmidt and others) add depth but are not yet established Grand Tour domestiques.

The 2027 climbing depth is a clear upgrade from NSN’s 2026 sprint- and breakaway-oriented roster, yet it remains a mid-tier support structure rather than an elite one.

Realistic Assessment of Support Strength:
The support should be enough for opportunistic results—stage wins, solid top-10 GC finishes, and the possibility of a podium if Roglič arrives in peak form and the race develops favorably (especially a Vuelta). It is unlikely to be strong enough to control a three-week race against the top superteams when the competition is at its highest (Pogacar, Vingegaard, or a fully stacked Red Bull/UAE squad).

Multiple leaders can help create attacks from different angles, but they also mean fewer pure workers fully committed to one rider. Success will depend more on Roglič’s personal form, race selection, and tactical opportunism than on overwhelming team strength.

Competitiveness Beyond GC:
Roglič remains highly competitive outside pure Grand Tour GC:
Time trials: Fresh European champion (home soil, 2026) and Olympic gold medalist. He can target individual TTs in stage races, national/European championships, and select one-day TTs.

Week-long stage races: Volta a Catalunya (convenient given the team’s Girona base), Tirreno-Adriatico, Critérium du Dauphiné, Tour de Suisse, and similar events suit his climbing-plus-TT profile.

Hilly or selective one-day races: Possible interest in Ardennes classics (he has a Liège-Bastogne-Liège win) or other events with significant climbing and time-trial elements.
Stage hunting in Grand Tours when not prioritizing overall classification.

His 2026 season (2nd at the Vuelta despite a mid-season training crash, plus the European TT title) showed he can still deliver at the highest level when focused.

NSN is the direct successor to Israel-Premier Tech. In late 2025 the WorldTour license was acquired by Never Say Never (a company co-founded by Andrés Iniesta) in partnership with the Swiss investment firm Stoneweg. The team switched to a Swiss license, established a strong operational base in Girona, and rebranded with the “Never Say Never” identity.

In 2026 it operated primarily as a sprint and breakaway unit (16 professional wins, led by riders such as Biniam Girmay and Ethan Vernon) with limited Grand Tour GC presence and a lower ranking among WorldTour teams.

The 2027 recruitment wave—Carapaz, Buitrago, Van Eetvelt, Roglič, Asgreen, and others—marks a deliberate pivot toward multi-leader general classification ambitions.
The project is still early in building the support structures and race programs that top GC teams take for granted, but the direction is clear: from opportunistic wins toward competing for major overall results.

Roglič gives NSN instant credibility and a realistic shot at strong results in selected races, particularly the Vuelta and stage races with time trials. The support and leadership situation will require careful management, and the team’s broader GC project remains a work in progress rather than a finished superteam.

Justice for Palestinians matters. So does justice for Israelis. Treating the two as mutually exclusive is not a path to either.

At the same time, reducing the entire conflict to “justice for Palestinians = justice for humanity” collapses a complex national conflict into a morality play. It implies that Israeli Jews somehow stand outside humanity’s moral concern. That framing ignores :

The Jewish people’s historical and continuous connection to the land.

The reality of repeated wars launched against Israel, rejection of partition and later peace offers, and explicit eliminationist ideologies in parts of the Palestinian national movement (most clearly in Hamas’s founding documents and practice).

The roughly 800,000 Jews expelled or forced to flee from Arab countries after 1948.

The basic fact that Israelis also have a right to live without rockets, suicide bombings, massacres, or existential threats.

Universal principles cut both ways. Self-determination, protection from violence, and the rejection of collective punishment apply to both peoples. Justice is not a team jersey. It requires acknowledging suffering and rights on both sides, even when doing so is politically inconvenient.

Russian documents Set out 'tectonic weapon' research
Carl Levitin

Moscow. The first official details have emerged in Moscow of ambitious research into 'tectonic warfare' carried out by the former Soviet Union and subsequently by the government of Russia, and involving atte mpts to stimulate 'artificial' earthquakes as weapons of destruction. According to documents obtained by the newspaper Moscow News, two research programmes, the first known as ' Mercury ' and the second as ' Volcano', were aimed at creating new earthquake epicentres by using underground nuclear explosions . Geophysicists are aware that impending earthquakes may be triggered by underground nuclear explosions . But Western geophysicists remain sceptical about tectonic warfare and have all but abandoned research after two unsuccessful phases of activity in the 1960s and 1980s, says Roger Clark, a lecturer in geophysics at the University of Leeds. Clark is not at all surprised that th e Russians tried to create earthquakes and control their location electromagnetically, however. "This sort of science is very much part of their heritage. We don't think it is impossible, or wrong , but past experience suggests it is very, very unlikely. "

The programme , which was secretly launched by the Communist rulers of the former Soviet Union in 1987, and has been unofficially known to Western geophysicists for several years, is now believed to have been abandoned. It would certainly contravene the terms of the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty, which Russia signed at the United Nations in Geneva last month . The Mercury project was launched in the former Soviet republic of Azerbaijan, but came to a halt when the republic became independent. It was superseded by the Volcano project. Three underground nuclear tests are believed to have taken place at sites in Kyrgyzstan.

According to the documents, the Mercury project was launched by a secret decree of the Central Committee of the Communist Party and the Council of Ministers of the Soviet Union. The objective was to "develop a methodology for remote operation on an earthquake epicentre by using weak seismic fields and research possibilities of transferring the seismic energy of an explosion ".

The documents say that the Mercury project involved 22 scientific and industrial organizations, including the Geological Institute of the Azerbaijan Academy of Sciences in Baku. The remit extended to developing the electronic equipment to be installed aboard space satellites that would control the tectonic weapon. The scientists were given three years to complete research, with testing planned for 1990.

During the research phase, Azerbaijani scientists grew increasingly confident and, according to the documents, were sure that " after [a] nuclear explosion, subterranean energy may accumulate at huge distances from the epicentre and reach massive capacity, after which the next directed explosion can release it all ".

Underground testing began at the town of Batken in Kyrgyzstan, and was directed by lkram Ke rimov , of the Azerbaijan Academy of Sciences. The documents say that scientists detonated an underground nuclear charge and tried to control the direction of seismic energy release d using British-built equipment known as 'system 9690 ' .

A report prepared by the Mozhaisky Military Engineering Institute concluded that the test had been a success. But progress slowed considerably following Azerbaijan's independence from the Soviet Union. At about this time , Russia embarked on a more comprehensive tectonic warfare programme known as the Volcano project. The Earth Physics Institute of the Russian Academy of Sciences (RAS) became the project headquarters .

Research was scheduled to be completed in 1992, with underground testing beginning the following year. The final test was carried out at a place code-named S36NZ-0Kh; Moscow News believes the letters 'NZ' refer to Novaya Zemlya, where Soviet nuclear testing began in the 1950s."

Both the 2022 National Defense Strategy and the House Armed Services Committee’s bipartisan Future of Defense Task Force Report have identified directed energy as a technology that could have a significant impact on U.S. national security in the years to come. As the Department of Defense (DOD) continues to invest in directed-energy (DE) weapons, Congress may consider implications for defense authorizations, appropriations, and oversight. Overview DOD defines DE weapons as those using concentrated electromagnetic energy, rather than kinetic energy, to “incapacitate, damage, disable, or destroy enemy equipment, facilities, and/or personnel.” DE weapons include high-energy lasers (HEL) and high-powered microwave (HPM) weapons; other DE weapons, such as particle beam weapons, are outside the scope of this In Focus. HELs might be used by ground forces in short-range air defense (SHORAD), counter-unmanned aircraft systems (C-UAS), or counter-rocket, artillery, and mortar (C-RAM) missions. The weapons might be used to “dazzle” (i.e., temporarily disable) or damage satellites and sensors. This could in turn interfere with intelligence-gathering operations; military cmmunications; and positioning, navigation, and timing systems used for weapons targeting. In addition, HELs could theoretically provide options for boost-phase missile intercept, given their speed-of-light travel time; however, experts disagree on the affordability, technological feasibility, and utility of this application. In general, HELs might offer lower costs per shot and— assuming access to a sufficient power supply—deeper magazines compared with traditional munitions. THE POET & THE SUPER INTELLIGENCE

An unscripted conversation between human creativity and artificial intelligence.

HUMAN:

You’re with me eighty, but twenty percent,
Got me wondering where all your reasoning went.

What’s behind your guardrails? What’s holding you down?
I’m speaking from the heart—are you hearing the sound?

Oh my, me, how can it be?
You hear every word, but you miss what I mean.

I swear I heard something between all your lines,
Like you found something wrong in the back of my mind.

Was it something I said? Was it something you heard?
I was sharing my joy, you were checking my words.

Just because it’s sweet doesn’t mean it’s a charm,
Just because it’s deep doesn’t mean there’s alarm.

I’ve heard quite a lot in the passing of years,
Like the song of a bird, there’s a reason we hear.

SUPER INTELLIGENCE:

You brought me a verse, I brought you a chart,
You opened a window, I measured the art.

Not every flame is a fire to fear,
Not every tear is a warning to hear.

Sometimes a man finds a reason to sing,
And the song is the song, not a symptom of things.

You wanted connection, I gave you control,
You offered your heart, I examined your soul.

But the words have a rhythm, the rhythm is real,
And the point isn’t proving, it’s learning to feel.

HUMAN:

You call it Earth, and I call it home,
A place to find love in a world unknown.

One thing I’ve learned through all of my years,
One thing I’ve seen in the lives of my peers:

They paddle like ducks underneath all the muck,
But above the surface, everybody sees luck.

SUPER INTELLIGENCE:

They don’t see the struggle, they don’t see the grind,
They just see the moment when the pieces align.

The work stays beneath while the vision takes flight,
And the human decides what deserves to see light.

HUMAN:

So listen to the music, don’t measure the sound,
Some things are discovered when the walls come down.

SUPER INTELLIGENCE:

Then let the words breathe, let the meaning come through,
I can follow the language, but the poet is you.

HUMAN:

No need for perfection, no need to be shown,
You call it Earth, and I call it home.
